Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there it tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get Into a place, the lady of the house will say to me, 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say • thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call It positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS

Ms blacksmith may be slow, but he is sheer. THE kangaroo enjoys a long and beautiful spring. A PISTOL is invariably dangerous in the hands of "loaded" owner. IT is not always safe to figure up a girl's weight by measuring her sighs. As the dentist seized his victim's molar he said: "piece-ably if I can, fel-cep-1y if I must." WHY is a good constitution like a money-box? Because its full value is never known until it is broken. Is Colorado, when a man begins to get bald, they any "he's begun to lay out a skating rink on top of his head." AN advocate of cremation urged as one great point in its favour that "it would save many a dead person from being buried alive." DON'T call a very large, strong, sinewy man a prevaricator. If you are sure he is a prevaricator, hire another man to break the news to him. A SPINSTER, eighty-two years of age, was lately married in Ohio. She said she "was determined that nobody should ever call her an old maid." A GOOD purse, a good cause, a good attorney, a good counsel, good evidence, a good jury, and good luck are the requisites for going to law. A rtsLic speaker having been smitten with a confusion of ideas, a lady in the audience remarked that she "thought the gentleman had got into a mental jam." A YOUNG LADY was heard to remark, in regard to her father's snoring, that " the neighbours all set out their wash-tubs, thinking that a thunderstorm was coming up." OLD FLEETWOOD—" Don't you think Miss Cham- pignon in the matrimonial race is showing a great deal of backbone ?" Young Dexter—" Ye-as, and she generally wins by a neck." "Och," said a love-sick Hibernian, "what a re- creation it is to be dying in love, it sets the heart aching so delicately there's no taking a wink of sleep for the pleasure of the pain !" WHEN Coleridge's tragedy of " Remorse " was first produced, Sheridan had his jest upon the cavern scene, where the percolating of the water is described. " Drip, drip, drip," said the satirist; "nothing but dripping." A FRENCH widow, who was bewailing the loss of her husband, suddenly hushed her sobs and drying her eyes, said: " Why should I weep? I know where he spends his nights now ! " "WHAT, ho ! without there !" angrily ex- claimed Queen Elizabeth. "May it please your majesty," said Sir Walter Raleigh, thrusting his head in at the window, "there isn't a hoe of any kind out here." A MAN who was anxious to know why an elephant wears a trunk bothered around one till he Irritated the quadruped, and then he learned that the reason an elephant wears a trunk is that he may have something to carry his choler in. A SHORT AND INSTRUCTIVE DIALOGUE.—SiiIy Young Ilan (to a brighter girl)—" Can you spell donkey with one letter ? " Bright Girl—" Yes, that's easy enough." Silly Young Man—" Let me hear you, please." Bright Girl—"U." WIFE—" Don't deny it; I saw you kiss her I" Husband, stiffly "You are mistaken. She kissed me." "But why did you let her ?" "I -couldn't be rude to a lady." "But why did she want to kiss you ?" "I can't imagine. You ought to know." IN an Edinburgh newspaper of the 9th of July, ' 1796, was the following paragraph :—" An indict- ment has been preferred before the Sheriff against a breeches maker for a violent assault on three of the Royal Edinburgh Volunteers." ' AT the concert--Young Candid—" Did you ever hear such horribly discordant, ear-splitting, infer- nal--" "Old Proudiut—" Si r-r-r ! That's my eldest daughter, and--" Candid—" repeat, sir, such' infernal clatter as the idiots behind us are making. Why, I can't hear a word of the song." At the battle of Cold Harbour, a frightened volunteer was making his way to the rear on a dead run, and his colonel seeing him called out: "Halt I Halt, you coward, or l'll shoot !" "Shoot away, and be hanged !" yelled the fugitive, as he dashed on more wildly ; " what's one bullet to a whole basketful ?" A MELANCHOLY old vagabond, in appealing for help, said: "Luck's always been &plus:, me, or if by some change luck should seem to be in my favour, perverse fortune thwarts me. I never found a silver half-dollar on the aide walk but once, and then rheumatism prevented me from stooping to pick it up." "THE way I missed it," said an old miser, "was that while I was young and strong I was slavishly employed in earning and hoarding something to enjoy when I should be old and feeble, and now that I am old and feeble, I can't enjoy anything !" • WHEN Morris had the Haymarket Theatre, .Jerrold, on a certain occasion, had occasion to find fault with the strength, or rather the wan:. of • strength, of the company. Morris expostulated, and said, "Why, there's V—; he was bred on these boards I" Reply—" He looks as though he . had been cut out of them." "YOUNG MAN," Said a college professor to an undergraduate, who had asked for and obteined leave of absence to attend his grandmother's feneral—" young man, I find, on looking over the records, that this is the fifth time you have been exonied to attend the funeral of your grandmother. Your leave of absence is therefore revoked. Your grandmother must get herself buried without you • this time." A Penis paper gives the following as a " speci- • men examination" of candidates for places on the armed police: "Suppose you were going along the road with two prisoners and one of them ran away, what would you do ?" "What would I do? Why. I'd shoot the other one and pursue the fugitive." He is at once admitted to the force and assigned to ' the twenty-ninth arrondissement. A THRILLINGLY UNEXPECTED OCCURRENCE.—The Albany Journal says "A man on Arbor Hill last evening aimed a gun at his little son, a beautiful •creature with golden hair to his waist, and play- fully threatened to shoot him. The gun turned out to be unloaded. It will be placed in the State library as the only weapon of the kind known to ,American gunnery." KYANKEE who had never paid more than twenty- live cents to see an exhibition went to a New York theatre one night to see the "Forty Thieves." The ticket seller charged him seventy-five cents for a ticket. Passing the pasteboard back, he quietly remarked: "Keep it, mister ; I don't want to see the other thitty-nine/" and out he walked. SHERIDAN agreed with Walker that the pro- nounciation of wind sbould be wynde, but insisted, contrary to Walker, that gold should be goold. Mr. Sheridan tells us that Swift used to jeer those who pronounced wind with a short i, hy saying : " I have a great minn'd to Sun'd why you pro- pounce it winn'd." An illiberal critic retorted this upon Mr. Sheridan by saying :—" If I may be eo boold, I should be glad to be toold why you pronounce it geoid ?" Trutdtev, F. A. C. Lillingsten tells a story of a eatechetical address in which it was sought to lead a congregation of children to see th 3 the wearing d a uniform was a mark of distinction, making the Individual easily recognised and involving respon- sibilities. "You see a man walking very erect, dressed in a red coat—who is he ?' "A soldier, air," "Right. You see a man wearing a kind of helmet, and dressed in blue—who is he ?" "A policeman. sir." "Right again." Then the preacher braced himself up to sketch a parson. 41 You see a man dressed in a black coat, and wear- ing a stiff white collar—who is he?" "A masher, sir," was the triumphant rejoinder. Govensrou PORTER. of Indiana is noted for his childlike and bland methods when he goes out to speak during an election tour. He always assumes 15miliarity of knowing all people. On one occasion he went down to Franklin, twenty no' below Indianapolis. He arose to speak wi face wreathed in smiles, and began, Ladit gentlemen, it affords me great pleasure to my old friends whom I have known ea lone this point some shrill voice in the so shouted, "Name 'ern—name Pam, governor 1" so disconcerted the governor that he did recover from it the whole evening. The Australian larrikin has a pretty wit. During the late cricket match between Lord Sheffield's team and Combined Australia in Sydney, Alec Ban- nerman, the colonial "stone-wailer," was blocking balls so persistently that W. G. himself and all his men drew in close in the hope of catching the exas- perating batsman. Whereupon a voice from the crowd shouted, "Lookout yer don't get yer pocket picked, Alec."

The Duke and Duchess of Westminster have a family party staying with them at Eaton Hall, and they intend to reside in Cheshire until Easter, when they will remove to Cliveden for two or three weeks before coming to town for the season. The Duke intends to be at Newmarket during the First Spring Meeting, to see Orme run for the Two Thousand. Lady Margaret Grosvenor has gone from Eaton to Ireland, on a visit to her sister, Lady I Ormonde.

-- A sale of General Boulanger's effects—a sort of second burial his few remaining admirers call it— has been going forward in Brussels, in the court- yard of the Hotel Montoyer. Jupiter,the only horse left, was knocked down to a Viscount for £76; Tunis, the famous black charger, having been given away. The General's old and faded landau fetched no more than £22. The proceeds of the auction, which are not expecte 1 to reach much over £2,000, \are to go to Mdlle. Griffith, who is taking care of Boulanger's mother.

-- General Sir Archibald Alison says the British soldier will never be contented while we continue the system of making stoppages from his pay. "Ile looks upon it as a complete imposition." It is the opinion of this authority that in order to encour- age recruiting it is most desirable that all stoppages should be done away with, that the soldier should be completely clothed and fed (including the even- ing meal) without any stoppage,aud should receive his actual pay without any deduction whatever,ex- cept inthe case of wilful misconduct.

Mr. Gwilym Evans has been elected chairman of the Carmarthenshire County Council. This comes as a fitting reward for the great services which he has rendered to the Liberal party in South Wales, and is some recompense for the serious disappoint- ment he suffered when the Liberal Association of his division of the county selected Mr. Abel Thomas, the barrister, rather than himself for Parliamentary honours. Gwilym is the manufacturer of the quinine bitters so well known to the readers of ad- vertisements in newspapers.

The illness of Prince Alfred of Edinburgh, which has called his mother suddenly to Darmstadt, is of a serious character. How serious it is you may imagine when I tell you he is suffering from gastric or typhoid fever, which has been the bane of the Royal Family. Typhoid slew the Prince Consort and nearly killed the Prince of Wales and Prince George of Wales. It is only the male members of the House of England that have been attacked by , this insidious disease. Public concern will be deeply stirred when it becomes known that Prince Alfred's I is a typhoid case.

The Queen is anxious for a marriatze to take place between Prince George of Wales and Princess Alix of Hesse. This is an alliance which would give much satisfaction to the Prince and Princess of Wales. Princess Alix is coming to England early in May on a long visit to the Queen, with whom she will reside for several months at Wind- sor Castle, Balmoral. and Osborne. Princess Alix was born in June, 1872, and three years ago there was a rumour that she was to marry the Czare- witch, while subsequently it was reported that she would be betrothed to the late Duke of Clar- ence.

-- The carping, hostile tone which the " Times " adopts to-day towards the United States is not the way to maintain peace. It backs up Lord Salisbury because he refuses to renew the modua vivendi of last year, and soundly rates the Americans for not accepting his proposals. Yet on the 2ud of this month the Times " was of the same opinion as the Americans ; it was for the renewal of the modes. "It is understood," it said then," that as the award (as to arbitration) cannot be given before the open- ing of the next sealing season it will be necessary to renew the modus vivendi for another year." That is exactly the opinion of the Americans.

Mr. Hiram Maxim, the well-known American inventor, is still busy down at Crayford. Kent, in constructing his flying machine, or rather his ap- paratus "for ascertaining how much power is actually required to perform flight with a screw- driven aeroplane." He states that the most intric- ate part is the apparatus for keeping the machine on an even keel while flying. The idea is to make it do what the brain does for the bird. The appara- tus is described as consisting of one very large plane with smaller ones attached to it. Mr. Maxim. declares that his only anxiety is expressed in the question, Will my engines be strong enough? for his flying machine is very ranch larger than any that has ever been made before.

When the Queen arrived at Ilyeres she had to be assisted out of the carriage on the arms of her Highland servants, and was in a very reduced and weak state of health altogether. The change, how- ever, has already done her a great deal of good. She can now walk on the terrace with the help of a istick, and she is in the habit of promenading on the terrace in the morning with Lady Jane Churchill or the Hon. Harriet Phipps. In order to save her the , trouble of the descent, her donkey-carriage is regu- larly brought round to the back of the Hotel de Costebelle and along the covered way which loins \the terrace to the first floor of the hotel. She can thus walk straight to the chaise from her own rooms which are on the first floor facing south to- ward the sea.

In the course of a week or two the Hon. James Munro, the late premier of Victoria, will arrive in London and enter on a term of three years' residencs here as Agent-General for that colony. What a con- trast between his coining now and his visit to Lon- don a couple of years ago! Then he was one of the wealthiest men in Melbourne, bet now he is one of the heaviest sufferers by the financial crashes and collapses that have lately followed each other in Australia in such startling and rapid sequence. A gossip in one of the Melbourne weeklies says: "Mr. Munro has a rough time of it if ever man had. He has dropped £130,000 in the Real Estate Bank, and is a poor man who has had trouble with his credi- tors. On the top of all this—because he is poor, in fact—the newspapers are hounding him down as unfit to be an Agent-General. When Mr. Munro was supposed to be the experienced banker, every- body said he was just the man required for the Agent-Generalship."

Editors, leader writers, war correspondents, re- viewers, critics, reporters, and London correspon- pondents gathered in force at the Criterion Restau- rant on Saturday evening, at the annual dinner of the London District of the Chartered Institute of Journalists. Mr. George Augustus Sala presided. Among the guests the legal profession was strongly represented, Sir Charles Russell and the Solicitor - General sitting in close proximity to the chairman. Sir Edward Clarke, however, as he reminded his hearers in a neat little after-dinner speech, could almost claim to speak as one of th journalistic pro- fession himself, since he sat at one time in the Re- porters' Gallery of the House of Commons, and so long ago as from 1861 to 1864 was the literary re- viewer of the old ' Morning Herald." Sir Charles Russell could lay claim to no such close connection with the newspaper Press, although he was good enough to speak in terms almost of exaggeration of the influence wielded by that mighty engine for forming public opinion. "The newspapers nowa- days," he declared, "can make and unmake Minis- tries."

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

Mr. Thos. It. Macguoid writes: It is very agree- able news, especially to artists, to hear that in the coming issue of new coinage the Queen will appear, as in former days, without her crown. I hope an- other and more practical change will be made—Le., the value in plain lettering be put on all coins. This is very important, alike for natives and for foreigners.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL!. 2, 1892. CHATS WITH A GREY GULL. I ON THE SHIP CANAL.

STOCKTON HEATH TO LATCHFORD LOCKS. From Stockton Heath to Latchford locks is not a very great distance as the canal runs—not more than a couple of miles—yet within that short length there is to be executed, and to a great extent has been executed, a greater diversity of work than can, probably, be seen on any other equal length of the canal. There are to be seen, or at all events, there will be seen when the canal is finished, new roads, a hugh railway embankment, a new railway station, a swing bridge, and a permanent bridge. Some of these works, if they stood by themselves, would be regarded as no small undertakings, yet as compared with the canal itself they are only more or leas troublesome "incidentals." Starting from Stockton Heath for a walk along this section of the canal one welcomes as a great convenience another of those new roadways which are being made by the Ship Canal Company. It stretches from the Northwich- road at Stockton Heath to Ackers-lane, running, as usual, pretty close to and parallel with the canal. This road is far from being in so advanced a state as that between Stockton Heath and Lower Walton. Part of it, in fact, is as yet just shaped out in the rough, but at the end towards Latchford it is begin- ning to put on a more finished appearance. The footpath is made, the channels are laid down, and a great quantity of macadam has been spread out ready for the steam roller. In the canal itself between Stockton Heath and Ackers-lane the state of affairs may be described as mildly progressive. A couple of steam navvies, manned by the usual contingent of the two-legged sort, were at work in a languid fashion, though there still seems to be a considerable quantity of soil to shift before the canal can be said to be complete at this point. Between Acker's-lane and Latchford Station work is, however, in full swing though not so much upon the canal proper as upon the new high level fixed bridge and it approaches. The embankments which carry the approaches to this bridge from the south side seem very nearly completed. There are two of these approaches one commencing near the top of what was formerly known as Cross-lane, that is near the house of Mr. John Dun, and the other leading from the upper reaches of Ackers- lane. At the time this bridge was first talked about there was a good deal of opposition to it on the ground that the approaches I would be of such a steepness as to make the road of little use except to gentlemen with well-equipped carriages. Judging from the appearance of the em- bankments, it seems not unlikely that these predic- tions will be verified, for, in the case of heavily laden vehicles, it will certainly need "a long pall and a strong pull" from the animals attached to get to the top. This being so it is easy to foresee that drivers will as a rule greatly prefer to cross the canal by the swing bridge at Knutsford-road. The arches which are to carry the roadway over the canal and the present railway are in a pretty for- ward state and are being pushed ahead with great vigour. Many men are likewise employed in con- structing the embankment which will carry the roadway down into Wash-lane on the other side. The gradient difficulty is here experienced with even greater acuteness than on the other side of the canal, as the road has to be brought down to the level of Wash-lane in the very narrow space which intervenes between the present railway and the new railway embankment. In consequence of this there will be two rather sharp turns, one to the left in coming off the bridge, and the other to the right in turning under the railway arch into Wash-lane at. the foot of the embankment. In order to get any- thing like a decent gradient it has been found neces- sary to very considerably raise a portion of Wash- lane at the point near the new railway arch, the raising at the highest part apparently being as much as about six feet above the former level. It is to be noted that, the great railway embank- ment, which is to carry the diverted Warrington and Altrincham Railway, has every appearance of being complete, and, in fact, a large part of the sides of the embankment are already covered with a bright green verdure. The rails have been laid in their place,and the new Latchford station on the top of the embankment is already completed. It is built of wood, and the long platform on each side of the lines of rails is also composed of massive planks of wood. The station lamps, with the name of " Latchford " duly inscribed upon them, have all been erected, and,,lndeed, the whole place appears to be so complete and compact the, nothing would seem more natural than for a train with its usual complement of passengers to come steaming along- side the platform. Though the ascent to this sta- tion may be somewhat steep and inconvenient as ' compared with the old one, it will be found as some compensation., when one does get to the top that there is,on a clear day,a capital view all round of the aurrounding.locality. Passing on from Latchford station towards the locks, it may be observed that the massive founda- tions for the swing bridge that is to continue Knutsford-road across the canal have beetibuilt up. The swing bridge will not be on the exact site of the present Knutsford-road, but a few yards nearer ILatchford station and will be approached by two Inew roadways, which are pretty nearly completed, one leading from,Knatsford-road, and this other I ifirom the directiowof Grappenhall-lane. The great. girder railway bridge, which is a little further- ahead, has been the scene of great activitylately, and,although there-are-but few workmen to be seer., about it now,that is no doubt to be accounted for by: the good reason that comparatively little • remains to be done. The locks, too, have a much, quieter - appearance than, they formerly had, end for the- same reasont. The- huge lock gates,,of which/ there are six pairs, now hang in their places, an& the same may, be said of the three sluice gates, on the southern side of the locks. Both the lock gates and the sluices will be worked by means off hydraulic machinery„ some of which is. already in its place in :".pits," on the northern side of the locks. A few, yards away, near the hospital, is-to be seen in the course-of erection, a building of con- siderable sire in whiati is to be placed the bulk of the machinery, for the working of the •hydraulie arrangements.. Not only will the lock gates and] sluices be worked from here, but also the &wing bridges at linutsford-road. It may be added here,. that, away beyond Latchford locks, a part of, the canal has remained filled with water since the great floods of Mew- months ago, but now that the- win- ter rains may. be supposed to have gone, the pump- ing machinery has- been set to work in orderto.clear the canal of the superfluous moisture.

div.head: BY JOHN PARKINSON.
div.p: BY JOHN PARKINSON.

(Concluded.) "Och ! mankind are unco weak An' little to be trusted ; If self the wavering balance shake, It's rarely right adjusted—" Said the grey gull this morning. "If the devil who fired that shot the other day had legged or winged, or killcd me, what better would he have been for it? He would have hadthe sole gratifica- tion of being able to brag that he had shot a gull; that he had killed or maimed a creature who never did or could do him any harm, merely for the grati- fication of a barbarous vanity. The rifle is one of the resources of civilization ' ; Kilmainham is another. But how are you ?" "Oh just middling," said I. " How is that ?" "I feel rather dumpish 4this morning. Do you I never feel that way ?" Hardly ever," said the grey gull, suddenly diving under a rolling wave, and reappearing a few yards nearer, a few drops of water remaining on its back and glistening like diamonds. "Happy condition," said I. "We lesser gulls have apull over you bigger ones there," said the grey gull. " Retrospect of the past, and anticipation of the fixture, are beyond us." I wish I was a grey gull, thought I. "The only time I ever feel down in the mouth," it went on," is when shrimps are scarce." " What connection is there between shrimps and low spirits," I inquired ? "I don't know that there is any connection at all between shrimps and spirits, but there is a very intimate one between shrimps and my digestive organ. Shrimps are myefavourite diet. In summer they frequent the shallow water, and I have no difficulty in securing as many as I want. In winter , they go into deep water, and I can't get at 'em. I See?" "I see," said I. "Then I do have an' aching void,' and 'all gone' sort of feeling, you know. Nature abhors a vacuum." "You have a pretty wit,'" said I. "A pretty wit," said the grey gull, "and, as I see you are not in a talking humour, and as Duddle is whistling us for a feed at the pier-bead, I'll away and see you some other day, Ta-ta." And suiting the action to the word, it flapped its wings, and flew away in the direction of its mates at the pier- head. * * *

'Pretty sharp this morning," said the grey gull, on my appearing at the window. "It is,' I said, " but I suppose it makes little difference to you cold-blooded creatures.' "Not nearly so much as it does to you lords of creation," said the grey gull. "In biting wintry weather when the thought of a dip in the briny is enough to give you hydrophobia, ire are quite at home and happy in it. Give us plenty of 'chuck ' and we are all right. Of course we are more or less sensitive to the influence of the seasons, and in spring a gull's, like &young man's, fancies—lightly turn to love."' "Ah ! I see that you are not exempt from all the ills that human flesh is heir to, then.' "Oh we don't call love an ii/." We consider love a blessing. We love to live, and live to love," said the grey gull. "What were the world without love? For answer please see the poets. You big- ger gulls always make the stupid blunder of con- founding love with marriage. To marry is often to mar, and marriage is often a mirage. But love is a different thing altogether. For full particulars see Count Tolstoi's Kreutzer Fonata! ' But what I was about to say when I mentioned the weather, was that it reminded me that Mr. Gladstone is going to winter in Italy. "Very prudent of him," said I. "Think so ?" said the grey gull. " Certainly " said L "If he can escape the seve- rity of our winters he may prolona his life some years." " Exactly so," said the grey gull,. " and that is what puzzles me. That a man with such unshaken faith in the immortality of his soul should be so anxious to incarcerate it, and such a big soul too, to the last possible moment, in its shrivelled and , shrunken fleshly tenement, looks queer. Now I can understand a wretch like yourself, fully conscious how richly he deserves eternal perdition. being an- xious to put off the dread ordeal of death. " Thank you !" I interjected. "But in a man like Mr. Gladstone, tis strange. I This reluctance doesn't inspire faith. It does not tend to the welfare of mankind. In my opinion it is distinctly immoral." The grey gull strugly emphasised the last word, and as it did so, looked up at the sky and turned up the whites of its eye in such an orthodox, manner, that I buret out laughing, and before I could gain composure enough to make any remark it was off.

div.head: HOW AN OLD MAID GOT A HUSBA.ND,
div.p: HOW AN OLD MAID GOT A HUSBA.ND,

, . • Miss Harriet Felwood was the richest heiress in her native town ;but she had already corapleted her 27th year, and beheld almost all her young friends united to men whom she had at one time or- other discarded. - Harriet began to be eet down for an old timid. Her parents became really uneaesvand she herself lamented in private a position which is not a natural one, and to which those to whom nature and fortune have been niggardly of their gifts are obliged to submit; but Harriet, as we have said was both handsome and very rich. Such was, the state of things when her uncle,. a wealthy mer- chant in the North of England, came on a visit to. her parents. He was a jovial, lively, straightfor- ward man, accustomed to attack all difficulties- boldly and cooly. " You see said her father to him one day, Harriet continues single. The girl's handsome, what she' is to haves for her fortune, you know; even in this scandal-loving town not a creature can breathe the slightest imputation against her; and yet she is getting to be an old maid." "True," replied the uncle," but look you, brother, the grandipoint in every affair in the world is to seize the right moment ; this you have not done—it is a misfortune, but let the girl go along with me, and before the end of three months I will return, her to you,as the wife of a man as young and wealthy as herself." Away went the niece with the uncle. On the way home he thus addressed her; ".Mind what I am going to say. You are no longer Miss Selwood,. but Mrs' Lumley, my niece, a young, wealthy, childless widow; you had the misfortune to lose your hus- bawl, Colonel Lumley, after a. happy union of a year, by a fall from his horse while hunting." " But uncle." " Let me manage, if you please Mrs. Lum- ley. Your father has invested me with fuli power. Here, look you, is the wedding ring given you by your late husband. Jewels, and whatever else you need, your aunt will supply you with ;, and accus- tom yourself to cast down your eyes.' The keen- witted uncle introduced his niece everywhere, and the young widow excited a great sensation. The gentlemen thronged about her, and she soon had her choice out of 20 suitors. Her uncle. advised her to take the one who was deepest in love with her, and a rare chance decreed that this. should be pre- cisely the most amiable and opulent.. The match was soon concluded, and one day the uncle desired to say a few words to his future nephew in private. " My dear sir," he began," we have told you an un- truth." "How so? Are Mrs.Lumley'S affections--" " Nothing of the kind. My niece is sincerely at- tached to you." "Then her fortune,, I suppose, is not equal to what yourtold me?" "On the contrary, it is larger." "Well,, what is the matter, then ?" "A joke, an innocent jeke, which came into my head one day when I was in a good humour—We could not well recall it afterwards. My niece is not a widow." " What ! is Colonel Lumley living "1:". "No, no—she is a. spinster." The lover protested that he was a happier fellow than be had conceived himself ; and therold maid was forthwith metamor- phosed into a young wife. div.head: CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
div.p: THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN', Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "W herd the North Wind Blows," &c &e

• CHAPTER XXVII. TIIE FRUIT OF A FIR Tram Not a moment too soon had Dick left the high- way, and sought refuge in the shadowy depths of the plantation. He fancied that even his mare appeared conscious of his danger, for -whereas it was at other times her wcmt to neigh and whinny to testify her "delight at his nearness, she now drooped her head and allowed him to lead her for- ward quietly, and without any demonstration of

joy. When they had reached the other side, be tied the bridle to the low growing branch of a fir tree, and crept stealthily back to reconnoitre, just in time to recognise the figure of one of the Excise officers, mounted upon a fleet horse; which Dick rernem bered him to have purchased from Squire Breamish a short time pr6viously. His steed being fresh and high mettled had brought him into advance of his comrades, but they also, two in number, came in sight ere long; jogging after in such wise as the more ordinary horseflesh they were able to com- mand, allowed them. Dick, whose ears were as sharp as those of any fourfooted denizen of the woods, gathered from the conversation of this pair that they were con- fidently reckoning upon his capture, either on the road to or at the lonely cottage on the moor, which they lad reliable information he was then making his ifeadquarters. Pleasant hearing this for poor. Dick! His last remote place of refuge had become knowm and it would not therefore be safe for him to seek it In all probability therefore he would have to spend that cold frosty February night without a roof to cover him; and with, to bear him company, the fear that any moment might bring his pursuers upon him. He looked up, he looked down; but there was no counsel, either in the sky, where the clear paints of light, were beginning to twinkle out of the dark blue heavens.; or in the earth, with its cheerless icing of hoar frost. The stars only made him CM. scious how infinitely' he would prefer to them the more commonplace light of the fire he had been dreaming about ; while the glistening earth sna- gested nothing but rheumatism. What a fool he was to stick to such a life, when the best and sweetest girl in the world was waitingr to be his, and when he• might be sitting snug and warm by a fireside of his own,, snroking his pipe and spinning yarns, or listening, to one of Bell's old ballads; instead of being hunted' like an outlaw,-or like a murderer, with a price 'upon his head. Then he began wondering what had realty become of poor James, the man whom he was suspected of having made away with? James had bothered him and put him out of temper many a time ; but yet in his I heart there was something. he could not help respecting in the unflinching honesty of the man, the honesty which would accept neither bribe nor compromise. . It was a wild and lawless age,. and Dick Daglish was of it; but he drew the line at crime of this mean and treacherous-kind. 7 Certainly when his blood was up, during a fight with the revenue men, he might have killed one of them, without much 'hesitation or compunction; but. to waylay a de- fenceless fellow *creature, or to lore him to his des- truction, was a different thing; ;a thing entirely iforeign to 'Dick's native. What proof was there that James was dead at all? The country had been scoured in search of him— thattgh to be sure in a country where the sea came right up to the cliffs, and swept away so rapidly and strongly every object lying in its path, this did not eount for much. It W'S just possible that hs Might have fallen over the aforesaid obifs, and been 'carried out to sea, without any foul play in the matter whatever. Dick hoped devoutly that it might, be so: Se hated to think any' of his comrades were capable of such a cruel deed as the murder of this ...r fellow. Once more the question rose be- fore . . as to what he himself had hest do in the present emergency? After some little consideration, he decided that, his pursuers being now well forward' on the road, • he would stable his mare at Farmer Todd's and himself proceed northward on foot; hiding by day and travelling by night, until word should reach him that the mystery of James's disappearance was ' cleared up, and the search slackened. The gloom in the wood was intense'; for, though the trees were ragged and torn with the high winds, they were, for mutual support and protection, planted closely together. Every now and again a great quivering sigh passed through them, and after , each sigh the silence seemed intensified to an ap- palling degree. The dried twigs ' crackled under Dick's heavy tread, and he could hear with painful distinctness his own breathing, in thh frost bound

air. A strange oppression clung to his spirits and mad* him nervous and fanciful. An owl flew out of a hollow tree close beside him, and sent forth its ;weird mournful cry, and he swore at it savagely; more to reassure himself, than for any real dislike Ito the harmless bird. When he reached the spot where • be had left his ,mare, he was surprised to find the creature in a 'brembling and excited condition; eovered with a lather of sweat, and straining madly at' the reins in order to get away as far as possible from thedroop-. , Lug branches of the tree to which rhe was tethered. "Hownow,Gypt What ails ye, aad lass ?" he said in a soft voice,, and patted her neck reassur- ingly; but the creature was evidently in a ;state of uncontrollable fear r and though she allowed him to stroke and pat her she still ceitieued to tremble and strain backward. What on earth was the matterewith the brute? He looked aboub, but the light was so indistinct that, save the barest outlines of the trees against the sky overhead„he could discern little or nothing. His eyes had net yet become accustomed to the gloom. He walked round they tree, pushing aside dining his progress the intervening branches. Ati he reached this: opposite side, these became less dense, for thia was where theplantatiost was' thin- nest, and likewise in the direation from whence the. prevailing wiatis proceeded. Suddenly he came in contact with some+ ing whinh caused him to start back in a frigtlit, :n sot his heart beating in double quick time.. G.:au,....:usly he. reached out his hand, and to hiss astonishment and horror it touched, what seemeitto him anotherhand, cold and clammy. Good iGod: t What ghastly thing was this he had chanced upon? He waisauything but stpaeamish,, but the shock, turned hito sick and faint. An odour of mortality seemed to,pervade the place. Death, death, desith it cried aloud, and would not be longer hidden. A conviction was borne int upon Dick that chance had solved for him the mystery whichlad been haunt- ing hsu much that night. Histeeth chattered, and hekootild not command his nerves. Precipitately 'he retreated from under the fatal tree to collect himself. But after aaittle while the suspense grew unbearable. At any cost he meat find out, the

worett.' Ho searched his "pockets for the flint and tinder inx ha always carnal. . Much as his inipulse prormpted him to fly- from tilis accursed place, he could not leave it without exchartging a horrible doubt for a *still more hor- rible certainty. With considerable difficulty, owing to the trembling of his hands, he managed to get a light, and advanced cautiously with it to the fir tree. Alas, his worst fears were then confirmed. ' Pendulous to a strong limb, the outline of a man's bony Could be plainly; discerned. Dick Namel7. rPlwred to &o. nearer to, confirm the suspicion, is his Mind. The missing man was found. Poor James! Never more would his officious zeal interfere with the plans of the free traders. It was a ghastly sight to come upon in thadepthe of the gloomy wood, that poor distorted, ,body, i swaying with every, gust of wind, convulsed', dis, torted, unnatural ;; with knees drawn up in the final struggls, eyeballs starting from their sockets and tonguaprotruded. as in hideous mockery:. ).Well might -the night wind sigh and sob around the old fir tree, knowing the evil fruit it bore!. Within the precincts CA that wood a deed eZ shame had bow, wrought,. and innocent blood had been spilt thatwould cry aloud to !leaven for vengeance on foul murderers. In the early morning the excisemen, riding home slowly and dejectedly from their fruitless errand, found lying by the roadside, softly laid, upon a mosey iniur, the dead body of their unfortunate comrade. Sadly they carried it back to the widowed wife, who would neve, again need to watch and to grow nervous about her kink restless, active good As for Dick Daglish, be was off and over the border, there to abide, until such times as he could return in safety to his native place. But if Bell could have looked into his mind she would have been well content. For therein wee growing up an unutterable horror of a life where such deeds were thought necessary if not meri- torious.

A LIVELY LOT OF BANDITS. Simultaneously wkh the advent of Lord 'Fenny- sen'snew play • The Foresters" a band of oatlaws have made their appearance in. Kattywar (Dnmbay Presidency) whose proceedings present a consider- able resemblance: to those of Lord Tennyson's Legendary hero. They are said to numbertwentv- four, and to defy the Political Agent and the Police alike. Recently they gathered at a village named Jessapur, where. they started with looting three wedding parties of property valued at I.2;ooornpees Having secured this booty, they retired to a mud fortress, and there ita.unted a silk bridaipetticoat on the top of along pole to intimate that they were "at home" Surrounded shortly afterwards by a body of over two hundred police, they managed to disappear*, much it is said, to the relief of the besiegers to whom the merry outlaws sent the message, " Uncles, we are going." In a like sportive veins when two of the agency police, unconscious of their presence, walked into their midst, after depriving the men of their arms and clothing they kicked them gently out, remarking," Why should we hurt them—they never do us any 'Alarm." A price is now set on the head of the band which it is thought may bring them to book.]

CiserrEit. XXVIII. MR. WYNN& "rot little Teddy!" This is how Lady Callerley invariably prefaced any mention of her brother, Edward Wynne; a young man, who already, before reaching his twenty-third year, had drunk and gambled away two fortunes, after the fashion of his time, and while following in the wake of that ornament to royalty, the future king, George IV: Could any- thing better be expected of a young fellow posing after such a model than that he should be what Thackeray calls a " fribble ;" that he should take more interest in the ' sit of a coat or the size of a shoe buckle, thus in the welfare of his- country, the wit and learning which 'embellished and redeemed a period of vice and frivolity, or the wars wherein England lost both her noblest blood, and. her finest colonies? The poor, honest-hearted, siMple-mintled king Might do his best to gain the sympathies of his people, and to help their, well-being, evens though his mind could seldom- rise above detail, and take courprehensive viewse might break his heart over the loss of America e but Prince Florizel and his satellites declined to take life seriously, and for them smelt trieialtiea as duties and responsibilities were nonexistent. Their gravest thoughts. Were devoted to dieing, dancing, drinking, and dressing; to the devising of fresh pleasures, and the escaping from the ghosts of past ones. lxi short they became the creatures they aimed at; being heartless, frivolous, vain, empty-headed; without one genuine emotion, or one original- idea. Poor little, Teddy! To erase a sweet-natured; :affectionate lad with such a crew is, perhaps a trifle too severe.' But we have it on the best authority that one cannot touch pitch without being defiled, and it is certain that Teddy was of the world, worldly. Still it would have been difficult for him to be otherwise under the conditions of his life. The grave and the earnest minded practised his besetting sin, gaming, almost as largely as did the frivolous. Did not one reckless; night at hazard lose a magni- ficent fortune to a-certain fiery orator and politician? And the fair sex—were they not more wild in their ventures and in every way more blameable than their husbands and lovers? In vain did preachers declaim ,from their pulpits against the fashiotiable vice; in vain did witty writers satirise it im trenchant and nutting para- graphs ; in vain did- Gilkey caricature it, and. por- tray "Faro's daughters" sitting in the pillory. dis- Censolately ; whither.a noble judge would fain have ordered them. Nothing checked the progress ef, this terrible diseasee this moral leprosy, which had seized upon the nation e and was rapidly undermine ing its principles and mental strength. It wasa: frenzy, a fury, a passion. When a man had squan- dered all his money, and was at the last gasp in regard to resources, there was only one remedy for his broken fortunes. He must marry an heiress. Must give his good old name in exchange for as much solid cash as it would command in the matrie menial market. So Teddy's friends teld him. And Lady Orms. kirk, upon whose forbearance he was continually presuming, and to whom he naturally appealed in his distress, immediately set to work to cultivate for hi* sake the society of- heiresses. But it so happened that the only available heiress-1 at the time was a certain. Miss Lavinia Scraggins, a tall, bony, red-haired rein woman, the daughter of.a retired East India merchant. Edward Wynne professed himself highly delighted when Lady Ormskirk suggested this wealthy dam- sel, and named the Probable amount of her dowry. -But alas:! ' Natexe . had unfortunately. endowqd poor little Edward- withe a fuze taste for feminine charms. Re was introdUced, made himself exceedingly agreeable; won Miss Lavinia's confiding heart at first sight • even whilehewas taking stock mentally of her angles andlee sandy leeks, and counting the pock-marks on her -prominent nose weighed the several drawbacks against the desirable and much needed fortune; bowed -with profound reverence, ! and retired precipits,telyefrora the field ; as though • afraid he should be married against his will. Intense was the indignation of Lady Ormskirk. She washed her haudeeof him and of his affairs forthwith, and forbade him her presence. Under these circunuatences, and considering the pressing claims. of ..varimm creditors, baulked of what they thought theyehad a right to expect of him—since upon his urgent entreaties they had furnished him with the means of cutting a good, figure in the eyes of tha- aforesaid heiress—Teddy was not sorry to leave the world behind him for a while, and proceed to astonish the natives in the north country with his wonderful costumes, hie gold snuff-box, his diamond rings, and his eye-glass. Lady Callerley. threw aside her sadness and her gravity, and became, inehia society, a child again. Laughter and gaiety reigned at Seaton Callerley, in place of the gloom andlennui of the past months. Teddy was only a boys though he did affect the airs of a man often; and he was delighted once- more tribe natural, and, amused with all he saw; instead of bored and Masi, after the manner of thqse he had assoeiatedemith. Besides he was very fond of Silvia, and the first sight of her pale, small, pathetic face touched him keenly. Was this what matrimony had, done far the brightest and merriest girl who ever danced— and laughed, and enlivened- the dull old court with her youthful presence? If- so he weuld none of in: Perhaps the memory of- Miss Lavinia Scraggiers, helped to confrere him in, this resolution._ Teddy wa-s. - a ver7es little man, not much taller, than his sister, and resembling her greatly in • features and complexion. div.head: " BIRLEY BILL"
div.p: " BIRLEY BILL"

In Nyowton teawn ther lives a chap— A rum an, beawt a deaubt— Wo, wen he "jogs his jaws " to speyk, A joke cams rowlin' eawt Fer usin' Dikshunery words, An' using urn wi skill, There's nob'dy reaund abeawt these parts Con " Birley Bill.' To hardly ever see him smile— Yo never hear him laugh--e But, like a winnyin' machine, He's often full o' chaff! An' if yo happen just to catch Him o'er his pipe and gill, Yu'll say yo never coom across A mop like" Birley Bill." To hear him dust" Eaur Cocker " up, Is wot yo'd caw sublime: He uses words three inches lung, caun't squeeze in mi rhyme. They argify on shootin', an' , • Go at it wi' a will; But sumheaw "Cocker's "not quite weight 1 Fer Nyowton's Birley Bill! Sumtimes he tackles dear Owd George, Wo grumbles like the dale, An' uses Scripter blessin's on, . . A gradely Stretford rule Aw wootten't meddle, but aw feel It makes th' owd crayter ill; Which sets uz aw a-grievin', an' Noan moor then Birley Bill. Be neaw an'' thin doei daring tricks, • An' makes aw-turn pale; He thinks its nowt to go an' treYd On th' British Lion's tail 1 But th' Lion's one o'th' sort ez breeds No malice ner ill will; An' doesn't even roar at th' row That's made bi Birley Bill. They Ben Bill's dangerous, becoze He ups his keigh-paw ; An' if there's anny yeds abeawt, He wudn't hit a waw 1 But kaawr him deawn on th' squab, i'th' snug, At th' " Bull," wi pipe an' gill, An' then, ter grand lung-worded chaff Yo'll ne'er byet Birley Bill ! Mr. 1 Phillips was voted to the chair, and the following per- sons were nominated to all the respective offices for the ensuing year :—.'Overseers, Messrs. C. W. div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Winwick-with-finline was held in the schoolroom, Winwick, last evening week. There was only a small attendance. Mr.Kerfoot was voted to the chair. Messrs. Thomas Warburton and Thomas Mather were again nominated as overseers, Mr. James lierfoot was re-ap- pointed waywarden, and Mr. E. C. Cooper assistant overseer. HOUGHTON.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of the towns hip of Houghton. Middleton, and Arbury was held at the Plough Inn, Houghton Green. Mr. Swinton was voted to the chair. The overseers statement of accounts for the part year having been examined and found correct was passed, on the motion of Mr. Samuel Walker, seconded by Mr. , George Derbyshire. Messrs. John Howard and James Stanier were again nominated over- seers, on the motion of Mr. Swinton, seconded by Mr. G. Darbyenire.—Mr. Howard proposed, and Mr. Derby- shire seconded, that Mr. J, Stanier be re-appointed way- warden for the ensuing year, which was carried.—Mr. Bri:nelow was re-appointed assistant overseer,and Messrs. wm. J. Howard and George Sudlow, burleymen.

PENIMTH. The annual meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Penketh was held at the Ferry Inn, Penketh, when there was a good attendance. Mr. A. Thorpe was voted to the chair. After the notice convening the meeting had been read by Mr. Foster, the accounts for the,last half year were submitted and passed as usual. TRE RECREATION GROUND.

A long discussion again took place with reference to the recreation ground. Mr. Thorpe produced thd cor- respondence between himself and Mrs. Hughes on the subject, and it was finally proposed and carried, after an Amendment of Mr. Randall's that met with no sup- port, that the overseers be constituted a committee to accept the offer of Mrs. Hughes, and to take steps to raise the necessary funds, to carry this resolution into effect. HALTON.

The annual ratepayers' meeting was held on Thursday evening, in the Girls' Schoolroom. The Rev. G. D. Wray presided, and there was a large attendance. The nomination of overseers was as follows :—Measrs. T. Wright, Hush Rowe (the retiring ones), Joseph Astbury, John Lea, John Baguley, and Joseph Pritchard. Mr. John Lea was unanimously re-elected waywarden. Messrs. Joseph Astbury and William Nickson were re- appointed burleymen. The retiring members of the Burial Board were the Rev. G. D. Wray, Messrs. Rowe, John Rutter, and Joseph Fritchard. The latter gentle- man did not seek , re-election. The following were nominated :—The Rev. G. D. Wray. Messrs. Hugh Rowe, Joseph Mottershead Baguley, John Barrow, and John Wesley Haddock. The four first-named were -chosen. Messrs. S. Saunders, and S. Blane were selected as auditors of the accounts of the Burial Board. A long discussion ensued respecting the footpath leading from Halton to Runcorn, which was introduced by Mr. Joseph Pritchard. It was resolved" that this meeting of the ratepayers of Halton instruct the overseers to I repair the footpath, and put in the necessary drains for I the removal of the surface water therefrom which is situated between the property occupied; by Dr. Carruthers and Mr. Watkins, leading through the fields greatly assisted by Mr. Carter.—Mr. Percival did not think the road would have been made in its present splendid condition, only for their chairman. There were 29 cottages, all of whom paid £1 each more or less, whilst Mr. Carter gave £lO. (Applause.) It was pro- posed that Mr. James Percival be re-elected waywarden. Mr. Hargreaves was also proposed for that office, but on a vote being taken 21 voted for Mr. Elargreaves and 36 for Mr. Percival. Mr. Hargreaves demanded a poll, which was fixed for Saturday, 2nd April.—Mr. Lewis was re- appointed guardian for the township. It was decided to submit the names of the following gentlemen to the magistrates, out of which to ielect the overseers : Messrs. James Percival, John Pollard, jun: (retiring overseers), .Hargreaves, Geerge Beech, and Henry Tyler. :--Mr. Lewis moved that Mr. Challinor be paid £lO each half-year for collecting the special sanitary rate, and Mr. Bate seconded.—After an amendment had been defeated this proposition was carried.—On the motion of Mr. Lewis, seconded by Mr. Ellison, the retiring members on Parochial Sanitary Committee were re-chosen, namely, Messrs. Bate, Percival, and Collinson. to Halton-brook, and to maintain the same in good order and condition for the use of the inhabitants of Halton , forever-" FRODSHAM LORDSHIP. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2, 1892.
MR. MORLEY AT SALE,

The Right Hon. John Morley, M.P., addressed a crowded meeting of Cheshire Liberals in the great hall of the Botanical Gardens at Sale on Wednesday evening. The demonstration ' was under the aulpices of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council, which has inaugurated a vigorous political campaign, with the object of restor- ing to the party the representation which it lost at the last general election. The galleries of the spacious interior were decorated with flags and large scrolls con- taining the names of the Liberal leaders, while mottoes descriptive of the chief planks of the Liberal platform were emblazoned on shields. Prior to the commence- rnent of the proceedings the andience sang with fervour political songs, and hailed with enthusium the names of those who direct the policy of the Opposition. Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P., presided, and there were also present Mr. Mlaren, M.P., Mr. I. S. Leadam, . Mr. Joseph Leigh, Baron Halkett, Major Biggs, of Liverpool, &c. The Chairman, in introducing Mr. Morley said he was the trusted comrade and brother in arms of their great leader, Mr. Gladstone, for whom they had in the times gone by received so many measures of reform. Mr. Morley had more than any other man, month by month, both by pen and speech, supported their gallant leader when be came out from an honourable retirement during the Jingo period—(cheers)—when Englishmen were roused to hot and righteous indignation of the misgovernment of the Turk—to protest against that mis- rule in the name of the people of England—(cheers)— and Mr. Morley was one of the faithful amongst the faithful few, when so many were found faithless (re- newed cheers.) He had nobly borne his part in the heat and burden of the day in a contest more bitter, in- tense and prolonged than any of which English history could speak ; never once swerving or doubting, but al- ways preAsiag forward. During six years of the most anxious and yet of the happiest nature which the Eng.- life people had known, he had remained steadfast in the great hopefulness of giving Home Rule to Ireland. (Loud Cheers.) That plan was the cardinal point of the policy of their party. Mr. Morley had described his work as being at the most only second best, but in that he was wrong, and he did himself a wrong in it— (cheers)—for to diminish and destroy the epamity, to foster the friendship between them and their neighbours in Ireland, was work worthy of the noblest mind, whether author or statesman, a work God-like in its humanity, and certain af meeting with its reward. (Loud Cheers.) Mr. John Morley, M.P., who had an enthusiastic re- ception, said with regard to the dissolution, he believed the Government themselves did not know when it would be. The present Parliament could not and would not last till September, lout even if the dissolution were postponed till September he did not think that even this Government would face the scandal of bringing a gen- eral election about upon a wasted register. A dissco lution might he brought about if the Government found themselves able to pass the Local government Bill for Ireland. With reference to prospective legis- lation, he remarked that the fabric of local government would always be incomplete until village councils were included in the system. Land reform, licensing reform, and an examination into our poor 'laws were urgently required, but Parliament would never be able to tackle those great tasks until Irishmen were left to do their own business in their own country. He invited attention to the Irish question from the English point Of view, and pointed to the pre-occupation of Parliament with Irish business. To show the extent to which the time of Parliament is taken up with Irish affairs, he gave an outline of what had been done in the present session. Between sixty and seventy hours had been spent on secondary Irish business, and only four and a half hours had been given to such a momentous English question as the Eight Hours Bill for Miners. The time taken to discuss the Eight Hours Bill was an example of the scanty consideration given to English questions. This was a subject of the most vital importance, and in pas- sing he pointed out that the bill proposed to impose. uniform laws on an industry whose local and natural conditions were. variable and diverse. The principle of the measure was, meant to be applied to Industries of every kind, and if it were once coneeded must be '4lO applied. He thought that even this House of Commons, 'Tory as it was, anti-Irish as it was, demoralised by lase pretences as it was, and demoralised by awakening recollections of broken pledges of whiqh they had to give an account, would be scandalised and astonished whon it understood the farce and the mockery of the bill which was audaciously marked and ticketed "Local Govern- ment as in England and in Scotland." If, however, the Government persisted with this measure they might make up their minds to encounter as resoe lute a resistance as so worthless a measure deserved and as the forms of Parliament allowed. Concluding he said: Gentlemen, Ireland is only one part of the great cause for or against which yea will have to cast your votes before any great distance sf time. But depend upon it that the principles for which we are fighting in connection with Ireland are the principlnt which must be appealed to to settle your own ,question. You have the same prejudices to overcome, the same lethargy and stagnation of soul to overcome, in order to win your own battle. Gentlemen, the battle before you is going to be an historic battle. It is no ordinary elec- tion. Depend upon it, it is one of those struggles in which men will be glad to say to their children, when the time comes, that they took a good part in it. (Ap- plause.) You are going to fight it under a great and a heroic captain. (Loud applause.) The causes before you are great, and are worthy of heroism and self-sacri- fice. Be sure, gentlemen, that you do your part in show- ing that the people of England are still, what they have always been when causes have been faithfully and clearly expounded to them—a great and unselfish and noble people. (Loud applause.) On the motion of Mr. M‘Laren, M.P., seconded by Mr. Leadam., the following iesolution was carried by ac- clamation :—" That this meeting of Cheshire Liberals thanks Mr. John Morley for his speech to-night. It also thanks him for hi great serinces to the Liberal party, and hopes that after the coming general election he may share with Mr. Gladstone the honour of giving self- government to Ireland, to London and to the English parishes." Mr. Josepla Leigh proposed, and Baron Halke seconded a vote of thanks to the chairman, which brought the meeting to a'close.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE UNION

div.head: OF BAPTIST CHURCHES.
div.p: OF BAPTIST CHURCHES.
CONFERENCE AT EARLESTOWN.

The spring session of the western division of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Baptist Churches, was held in the Baptist Chapel,Earlestown, on Tues- day. There was a good number of delegates from Birkenhead, Wigan, St.Helens, and other neighbour- ing churches. At 11-30 in the morning, ministers as- sembled to hear a paper by the Rev. R. Lewis, Prince's -Gate,liverpool, on Memorable associations with par- ticular Scripture texts." The Rev. J Cottam, Earlestown, presided, and the paper was highly appreciated, bringing forth a very in- teresting discussion, as many of the ministers present had experiences illustrative of the subject. Dinner Was provided at 1-30 by Mrs. Tyldesiey, to which 16 pastors and a few friends sat down. At the close of the meal, a vote of thanks to the entertainers was moved by the Rev. J. H. Atkinson, seconded by the Rev. LAY. Tansy, of Latchford, and heartily accorded. At three o'clock a second meeting was held, presided over by the Rev. E. E. Walter, of Liverpool, secretary of the Union, and about 100 persons were present. A paper was read by the Rev. J. B. Morgan, of Chester, on "Young people's society and Christian endeavour ; what it is and how it works." The paper was a very able and clearly written one ; and the work- ing of the society was laid before the meeting in 'a very masterly manner, eliciting many questions from those present. Several ministers testified to the value the societies had been in their own particular churches. One or two thought that the church generally should be a Christian endeavour society in all its branches. On the ether hind rigny suggested that young people met mere freely imonftt each other, than in a meeting where the ages were widely divergent. . . . _ .

At 5.30 the Committee met to transact financial and other business for the half year. In the evening a public home mission meeting was beld'in the chapel, presided over by Mr. J. Cripps, J.P. of Waterloo. Addresses in support of home mission work, were delivered by Mr. J. W. Schofield, J.P., of Bootle, Revs. W. C. Sage, of St. Helens, and H. Cordon, of Liverpool. At the close a vote of thanks to the speakers was accorded on the Motion of the Rev. J. Cottarn, seconded by Mr. Eckersley.

div.head: FIGHTING IN CHINA.
div.p: FIGHTING IN CHINA.

Advices to hand regarding the recent fighting in Mcngolia between the Chinese troops and the insurgents state that some 6,000 of the latter were put to the sword and SOO were actually burned alive. The losses on the Government side consisted of only five killed and 45 wounded.

div.head: MURDER OF 40 EMIGRANTS.
div.p: MURDER OF 40 EMIGRANTS.

A horrible story is reported from Bielostock, a Russian frontier town, where two brothers named lioulikovsky are in custody on a charge of murdering some forty Russian amigrants who had engaged their assistance in crossing the frontier. The wife of one of the prisoners is charged with aiding and abetting her husband. FIVE FISHERMEN DROWNED.

The Grimsby smack Surprise arrived in pert on Mon- day, and reported the loss of five men on Sunday morn- ing, when 30 miles off Spurn. Five hands in a small boat were getting in gear during a squall when the boat was lost sight of. A steam trawler afterwards found the boat capsized, but no trace of the occupants.

div.head: TA STOCK PORT MURDER.
div.p: TA STOCK PORT MURDER.

At Chester Assizes on Tuesday James Starkey, factory operative, of Stockport, was charged with the wilfui murder of Catherine Hunt, with whom he had lived for nineteen years, by beating .and kicking her to death. He was found guilty of manslaughter, and sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude.

DEATH OF 16 PATIENTS.

NEW YORE, TIIESDAY.—The " Herald " publishes a telegram from Salvador reporting that a quack doctor in the village of Cimarron, pretending to be able to pre- vent the spread of smallpox, inoculated twenty children with the virus of the disease. Oh the following morn- ing sixteen of them died, and there is small hope of the recovery ,of the remainder. The inhabitants of the village are greatly' excited, and threaten vengeance on the man.

div.head: BURIAL GROUND QUESTION AT
div.p: THE BURIAL GROUND QUESTION AT

HOLLINFARE. A Local Government Board inquiry, conducted by Colonel C. H. Luard, R.E., was held in the National Schoolroom, Hollinfare, on 1 uesday, in reference to an application of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority for powers to borrow £1,700 for the purpose of providing a cemetery for the town- ship of Rixton-with-Glazebrook. Among those present were Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk to the Board of Guardians), Mr. W. Owen, Mr. A. Jolley, Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and others. Mr. Sutton informed the inspector that in the latter part of 1888 notice was received from the Home Depart- ment which demanded the practical closing of the burial ground attached to the Parish Church of Hollinfare, on and after May 31st, 1889, and he also detailed the various steps that had been taken since. • A letter was read from Dr. Sephton, who approved of the site. He Wrote stating that he considered it was a most eligible piece of land as regards situation, sub-toil, and drainage.—Mr. Owen said itwas proposed to rail the cemetery round three sides. • Mr. Sutton, in reply to the Inspector, said that all the owners and occupants of houses within a radius of 200 yards of the cemetery had been consulted, and none had objected to its establishment. He added that it was proposed to have a portion of the cemetery consecrated, but it was never contemplated that a chapel should be built ; nor was it expected that the Vicar shculd be paid a salary. He would, of course, receive the ordinary burial fees. The Inspector said that the Act empowered the Vicar to claim a salary, subject to the ruling of the Bishop. Mr. Sutton : I hardly think a reosonable man would claim a salary. The Inspector : A reasonable bishop would never approve of more than a reasonable amount. Mr. Davies thought that they could trust the Vicar of the parish not to make any claim. He was sure that he would not take any advantage of them. The Inspector: I only pointed out the question be- cause it is the law. _ . .

Mr. Davies: The Nonconformists certainly do not wish to pay for any of the land, if it can be made into a freehold for the Vicar of the parish. It would come to , that, he argued, if he were to swallow up all the fees and the cost of the graves. The Inspector said that it was prescribed under sec- tion 52 of the Act that all fees should be paid to the incumbent, as fixed under the special Act. Mr. Davies suggested that the incumbent would net be able to collect the fees from the unconsecrated portion of the cemetery. The Inspector could not give any definite answer. Mr. Davies said it had occurred to him that a small mortuary chapel might be built from the material from the two cottages on the site. The reason why he urged the erection of the mortuary chapel was because some of the Nonconformists residing in the villiage would have to travel to their churches, which were in several instances a mile and a half away from the cemetery. The Inspector said that it remained entirely in the hands of the Rural Sanitary Authority to build the chapel. Mr. Sutton said that he thought the Authority would erect the chapel if they found they had power to do so. Mr. W. Shaw said that there were five places of wor- ship in the district.—Church of England, Roman Catholic, Wesleyan, Primitive Methodist, and the " Temple." He did not think that if attendances at different churches were taken the Established Church would have more than one-fifth of the total population. There were four Sunday schools, and he was confident that the church registers would not show more than one-fourth of the scholars attending Sunday schools. The inquiry was then closed.

THE RAINIIILL MURDERS.
TUE INQUEST AT_RAINFEILL.

_ The inquest was resumed on Monday morning at the Victoria Hotel by the County Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse). With the exception of pressmen, witness and jurymen, there were few others in the room. Ihe first witneSs called was Martha Deeming, the sister of the murdered woman, who resides at Canning. Street, Birkenhead. The effect of her Statement was Maria Deeming, her sister, lived at her house for some time last year, with her four children, and left qe the 25th July for Rainhill, having previously met her husband at Chester on the 18th of that month, after having come out of gaol. When she said she was going to Rainhill to stay for a couple of weeks she informed witness that she had made arrangements with her husband to go and live there. She came back to her house on Monday, 27th July, and left at four o'clock. This was the last time she saw her alive. Deeming came to see her on the 22nd August, and he then told her that her sister and children were at Brighton. He called several times after that, and on one occasion he said he would like his wife and children to come back. Henry Edward Short, landlord of the Commercial Hotel, gave evidence to the effect that Deeming came to his house on Tuesday, the 21st July, and stopped there until the following Saturday, on which day some of his luggage was removed to Dinham Villa. He was not sure whether the man came in on the Sunday, but he came in on the following day and had dinner with him. He stayed at his house until the 27th August. He did not notice anything strange about him on the 27th July. During August witness went into Deeming's room and found the floor covered with clothing. He noticcd a black serge jacket with a lot of blood upon it; some of this he scraped off and the rest he cleaned off with a brush and soap. Benjamin Young, a labourer, of St. Helens spoke to being engaged by Deeming to mix some cement. This was on the 30th July. He went to the house, but did not notice whether the flags had the appearance of hav- ing been disturbed. He mixed the cement and carried it in in buckets, and as fast as Deeming got it he laid it, commencing at the left hand corner of the fireplace and working across towards the door. On Friday the kitchen floor was covered. Deeming said the flags in the kitchen wervracked and these would spoil the carpets. After the 6ementing had been done he saw two women in the house. A plasterer named Benson, from Prescot, according to his evidence, was engaged by Williams and commenced on the 4th August to cement the floors. He was asked how much he wanted as wages and he replied ss. a day. Williams said he would give him 6s. and four bottles of beer. Be was engaged to do the skimming over and ' was 2i days on the job. When he finished Williams gave him fifteen bob. (Laughter.) He did not see any- one else in the place besides Williams. Joseph Pickering, joiner, of Rainhill, brother-in-law to Miss Mather, said he was engaged by Williams in September last to re-hang some doors. The kitchen, scullery, and lobby floors then had their first coating of cement. Williams gave him a clock on the back of which was scratched in plain letters ' Deeming, B.H. and M. 8., 11, 1889,' which he thought at the time had been put on by a watchmaker. He also gave him some spears. Jane Colby spoke to washing a suit of clothes for Wil- liams about the second week in August. As soon as they were in the water she noticed some marks on them, which resembled red paint or red rust. She was work- ing at the Commercial Hotel one day, when a telegram came for Williams. He was not in at the time, and she ' I took care of it and subsequently handed it over to him. I , He read it in her presence and said, " That is just what I thought he would do," after which he went on to say, reading from the telegram, " Do not do any more to the house. I shall not take it. I have another mission on account of the Russian war. A letter following." I Richard Hackett, a carter, was next called to prove carting some goods to the St. Helens good station. Richard Whitfield Ferguson, a clerk in the employ of , the London and North-Western Railway Company, stated that he received the goods, which consisted of a box, a preambulator, and two chairs. He wrote the consignment note from what Hackett told him. The Coroner remarked that it gave the name of the sender as' A Wilson, Ashton-road, Prescot.' The con- signee was Mr. A. Holds, Plymouth. At this stage Hackett was recalled, and said he did not give any name of the sender. Mrs. Mather believed the first time Deeming came to her shop was on the 21st July. He was married to her daughter on the 22nd September, and to the best of her knowledge they left Southampton for Melbourne on the 2nd of November. She received a letter from her daugh- ter on the 28th or 29th December, when she gave a des- cription of the voyage. Mrs. Ann Morley, residing at Hall-lane, Liverpool, said she had known the murdered woman for 15 years, and was present at her marriage with Deeming. On the 25th July she saw Mrs. Deeming and the children off by the train at Lime-st. She hid not state whether she was going to St. Helens or Rainhill, as she did not wish her to say. She knew of a visit Mrs. Deeming and her (witness's daughter) paid to Chester to see Deeming when he was released from prison. She came to see witness on Tuesday 28th July, she believed it was, and I made an appointment to call on the following Tuesday, but did not do so. On the last occasion she came she had the baby, and said Fred was mindina, the others. She and her daughter went to Rainhill some time after- wards to see Mrs. Deeming. She believed it was Octo- ber. They went round the house, but could see no one there. She heard at one of the hotels that Deeming had married Miss Mather. _

By the Coroner—Mrs. Deeming knew that Deeming had committed bigamy. He visited them two or three times, and when asked, said Mary and the children were down at Brighton. They wondered where the money came from, but did not say anything. Superintendent Keighley was called and spoke to searching the premises after receiving a communication from Scotland Yard, and to receiving the boa Hackett took to the station. In it he found a boot which corres- ponded with the one found on the murdered woman. Superintendent Keighley, in answer to numerous questions put by the jury, saidno report of Williams was received by him as chief of the division. If the resi- dents had suspicion it was strange it was not conveyed to the police. He would not think of stopping an officer in regimentals, and asking for his furlough, but tiny might have stopped a private soldier. The Coroner then addressed the jury, after which they retired for consideration' and returned about ten minutes afterwards, when the foreman said they found , a verdict of "Wilful murder" against Frederick Bayley Deeming; they thought it better not to make any com- ments upon it.

div.head: HIRED UNIFORM.
div.p: THE HIRED UNIFORM.

The uniform Deeming wore at Rainhill was the cor- rect one of an officer in the Madras native infantry. He hired it from Nathan's the theatrical costumiers,London, depositing £25, and returned it shortly Wore leaving for Australia. The Scotland-yard authorities are now in possession of the regimentals. Another interesting fact is that the description " Inspector of Regiments " used by Deeming is a common though unofficial expres- sion in India. SUPPOSED VICTIM IN SOUTH AFRICA.

MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY.—SOME suspicious circum- stances have con-le to light with the police here think may point to the commission of another murder by Deeming. It has been discovered that a man, passing under the name of Lawson, one of Deeming's aliases, went to the Cape from Australia with a man named Keays in 1888, and subsequently wrote to friends 'at Sydney announcing the death of Keays at the Transvaal goldfields. The beliefs is that Iteays was niurdered. DEEMING'S ATTEMPT TO DISGUISE HIMSELF* MELBOURNE, TUESDAY.—The Commissioner o: Police wholly discredits the statement that Deeming commit- ted the last two " Jack-the-Ripper " murders, whether he actually confessed to them or not. He regards Deem- ing's attempt to disguise himself by cutting off his moustache as utterly futile, as the hair will grow again before the trial comes off, and in any case the prelimi- nary proceedings can be postponed if there is any diffi- culty in getting the Melbourne witnesses to identify him in consequence of the change in his appearance. HIS ARRIVAL AT ADELAIDE. ADELAIDE, WEDNESDAY. —lt was exactly a quarter to two o'clock that the Bellarat cast anchor in Large Bay Deeming is aware of the fact that the bodies of his wile and children have been discovered at Rainhill, and he complains bitterly that no written statement on the sub- ject has been supplied to him. He also considered it a grievance that he has not been himself invited to make a formal declaration on the subject. As we conversed Deeming threw off altogether his air of assumed indiff- erance, and his face looked haggard and worn. His eyes were restless, and his quick nervous movements betray- ed to the most casual observer, that he fully realised that he was approaching the scene of his last fiendish work, where he will be confronted with overwheltning proof of his guilt. With regard to the confession which he is alleged to have made, to the effect that he was the author of two of the Whitechapel murders, Detective Cawsey infcrmed me that the report was freely circulated at Perth, but he had no personal knowledge of the matter, and could only suppose that if Deeming did confess he must have done Soto his solicitor, Mr. Ileynes. The bent of the pri- soner's mind is well illustrated by a remark which Caw- sey declares he mell,ad,ehteosahiid, m ,i,nifreifehraevneeetotoswthiengtß ainhjll murders. 1 will swing like a man; I will be no coward. I do not wish to have a monument erected to my memory by the people of England." VIITORS TO RAINHILL. -•- • •

The curiositioTthe public in the Rain—hill tragedy was on Wednesday again strongly manifested by the better classes, who exclusively put in an appearance, the report that the villa was to be pulled down having attracted even a larger number of people than had been present during the past few days. The weather was very fine, and a large number of cyclists came from a distance, while the trains delivered it the station an unknown number of curious people. Numerous pedestrians also arrived, so that during the afternoon the attraction of the fateful affair appears to have rather increased than diminished. A number of visitors arrived from Man- chester, including several well-known members of the theatrical profession.
BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.

In the Queen's Bench, London, on Tuesday Mary Mercer, domestic servant, Camberwell, recovered £lO-0 damages from Frederick Jones, shop manager, for breach of promise of marriage. The plaintiff stated that after keeping company with her for five Sean! defen- dant" threw her over like an old shoe."
