div.head: EXECUTION AT CHELSEA..
div.p: EXECUTION AT CHELSEA..

James Noble, 46, sweep, was executed •iu Newgate ' Gaol, at nine o'clock on Tuesday morning, for the mur- der of Mary Elizabeth Swift, a married woman,. with whom he cohabited at Chelsea. On February 4th. Noble and the woman returned home after having visited several public-houses, and a quarrel ensued, in which the man cut the deceased's throat. When charged, Noble said, " This is all through jealousy.' Billington was the executioner. He allowed a drop of seven feet, and death appeared to be instantaneous.

div.p: " Leaves of Grass" when Emerson, the greatest of American thinkers, could say of it :—" I find it the most extraordinary piece of wit and wisdom that America has yet contributed." It certainly stands alone in its daring self-revelation ; but its chief merits in our eyes are in its exaltation Of labour and the labourer ; in its bold democratic teaching, and the emphasis it lays on the brother- of man. WHITMAN was no sham in this matter ; he practised what he preached. He worked himself almost into the grave during the Civil War in nursing Northern and Southern soldiers alike, contracting paralysis from which he suffered -t° his dying day. His presence was helpful and ,cheering whilst he lived to many who were Bruised and maimed ; and we cannot but think that .hia writings, now that he is dead, will be stimulat- Ing and inspiring to many who are bruised men- tallY, whilst groping their way in life. It may be said of his peculiar chants as he himself says of 4` this broad earth of ours" : Amid the measureless grossness and the slag, Enclosed and safe within its central heart, ifestles the seed perfection. .Elere, in another couplet, is a hint and a wise *le too 110,„ see the secret of the making of the best persons ; is to grow in the open air and to act and sleep with the earth. Of himself he says :- 4 rnYself write but one or two indicative words for the 1, future, nut advance a moment only to wheel and hurry back the darkness. Perhaps the most popular of Whitman's writ- Ingll is his dirge on the death of Lincoln; and this 474 because it is superior in thought as because, °nce, his verse is rhymed, as will be seen from the following stanza : ?bee alna my Captain! our fearful trip is done; has weather'd every rack, the prize we sought +-3 Won. port is near, the bells I hear, the people all exult- -144 'follow eyes the steady keel, the vessel grim and daring • But d heart ! heart ! heart ! 0 the bleeding drops of red, Where on the deck my Captain lies, Fallen cold and dead. It will be seen that if the poet did not write verse in the ordinary style, it was from no w.itek of capacity for expressing himself in this Re preferred speech which was like himself ‘ngged and direct, so that he might say at the V!osB_

i, Camerado, this is no book, 4,.., Who touches this tcuchesa man. uu, after all, what we want is, n all cases, to get .14 the rnan behind the book, for sincerity covers i "13aultitude of defects. "Leaves of Grass" may ' 14:43"t1r become popular; but it will not perish, I110e8:118e it is sincere, and it is manly. The work is si ''. l'eadily accessible in this country; but the bulk 4iiit Illay be obtuined for a shilling in the Canter- t37 Poets series published by Mr. Walter Scott.

"TOUCH AND GO."
Another simile of the sea. At Blackpool, the other day, a young lady compared the breakers-to rolled gingerbread. She is a " sweet " creature.

"Fame," a smartly-written" journal for- adver- tisers," continues to give useful hints. Here is: one :—" A good article backed by proper capital, pushed with perseverance and faith, and made widely known to the public, without paying too exorbitantly for the publicity acquired, is. sure to succeed. This is no accident, it is an axiom !"

A Tory writer in the " Standard" is-, quite in- dignant because the Liberal Unionist candidate for South Edinburgh has accepted the principle of a graduated income tax. But what then ? The time will come when the Tories will try to make it appear that they were always in fa.•;our of the proposal ; but that will be when they can no longer resist it.

The Emperor William is a very determind young man ; but even he cannA have all: his own way. He has had to drop the Education Bill; and,, on Tuesday, the Reichstag refused the money for a new corvette. The Germans mean to count for something in the scheme of things as well as. their Emperor. They intend to contest "the right divine of Kings to govern wrong."

To " convey "an odd fern from a wood may be tolerated, but when it is a case of taking ferns wholesale to be sold retail the owner is justified in calling in the police. James Dory was brought before the Axminster magistrates, on Tuesday, and sent to gaol for fourteen days as a fern pilferer. He meant business, for when he was taken he was found to have cleared a space of two acres, and possessed himself of 1,080 fern roots.

Dissent is alive inßixton. The township is to be provided with a new cemetery; and in the course of the Local Government Inquiry, on Tues- day, a plea was put in for a mortuary for the Non- conformists. It was stated that there are three Dissenting places of worship to one Church of England and one Roman Catholic. Under the circumstances, it is extremely likely that the ap- plication will be favourably considered.

When Mr. Sutton remarked that it was intended to have a portion of the cemetery consecrated, the Inspector pointed out that the Act empowered the Vicar to claim a salary, subject to the approval of the Bishop. This, we find on referring to the Act, appears to result as a consequence of consecration. But there is no obligation to consecrate; and those in authority would do well to mind what they are about. The present Vicar may not seek a salary, but who can decide for his successor P

A question on the vexed matter of "Election Expenses," was put in the House of Commons, on Monday, and the answer of the Attorney-General was that "The expenses incurred by Parliamen- tary itandidates in respect to an election must, ac- cording to the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Pre- vention Act, 1883, be included in the return to the Returning Officer, irrespectivs of the date when incurred. No distinction was made in the statute between a sitting member and a candidate."

According to this interpretation of the law, a candidate selected, say as far back as 1886, would have to treat every meeting that he attended in the constituency adopting him as an election meet- ing. And so with the sitting member; every meeting held to give an account of his stewardship would have to be scheduled under election ex- , penses. But this is absurd; and if it is the law ' the law will have to be altered. The common- sense view of the matter is that election expenses should date from the hour when it is known officially that there will be an election—that is when a bye-election becomes necessary, or when a dissolution of Parliament is announced.

The late Mr. Spurgeon has left in personality and estate over £20,000. He must have preached at one time or another from texts which go to show how hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of heaven. A question which naturally arises is—How did he reconcile his preachirg in this case with his practice? Or are we to understand that he did not regard himself as a rich man ? Or, to raise another supposition, was it that he was willing to lay up treasure on earth, and, like so many other people, risk the hereafter?

Mr. Chamberlain's National Pension Scheme is not making headway. Mr. A. J. Fowler, of Ever- ton, writing the member for West Birmingham says :—" As one who gave evidence before the last Select Committoe on Friendly Societies, I bog to state that, in my travels and communications, I find that paying £5 at the age of twenty-five and RI a year afterwards up to the age of sixty-five to receive a pension of ss. per week afterwards is far from being popular." Mr. Fowler suggests pay- ing sixpence per week from 20 years up to 50 years, but is this any more likely to be popular? Enthusiasm was roused to a high pitch at the Liberal demonstration which was held at St. Helens on Monday. 'There was a time when the Tories would have had something to say about having on a Liberal platform an ex-convict in the person of Mr. Michael Davitt. It marks the growth of the Home Rule movement that Liberals honour the man who has suffered for Ireland, while Tories look on and are chap-fallen. It marks the growth, too, of the "union of hearts" —let the cynics sneer as they will—when a poli- tician of Mr. Davitt's stamp can forgot and forgive all that he has suffered and help Englishmen to secure a majority at the next election.

There is no verification of the rumour from Australia that the demon Deeming has confessed 'to having been guilty of two of the " Jack-the- , Ripper " murders; and a comparison of dates shows that he was not in England at the time, After the inquest at Rainhill, on Monday, he has quite enough to answer for. The mystery is that, with every appearance of a lying adventurer, he should have gulled so many people. It is not very likely that he will again set foot in this country, for,if the charge of murdering his wife in Australia be proved, he will be hanged on the charge. Assuming his guilt, it is better so. A revival, three months hence, of the details of the Rainhill murders could serve no good purpose ; the public have surely supped full of these horrors.

Mr. John Morley, in his speech at Sale, on Wed- nesday, paid a high compliment to Mr. Leadam when he said :—" I have known him a long time, and I may say, perhaps you have found it out already without my saying it, that he is a man by education, by talent, by capacity, by his most in- dustrious political work, not only here as a candi- date, but on many other fields, he is a man whom you may be very proud to return." Could anyone say as much of Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, without being thought "kinder sarcastic ?" The electors of the Altrincham Division of Cheshire will have the opportunity given them before long ef choos- ing between chalk and cheese; and, as they are Cheshire folk, they ought to know which is " the cheese."

Mr. Morley hit the nail on the head in his usual style when he spoke of the Tory programme as" a blank sheet"; and he neatly described their method when he said "They will go through the process, familiar with the Tory party, of dropping buckets down into empty wells, and bringing no- thing up." But his exposure of the futility and mockery of the Irish Local Government Bill was the main purpose of his speech, and that was ac- complished in style which must maim Mr.. Balfour wince. He finally represented the situation in a single sentence :—"The Government in these mat- ters," he said, "have trusted to the ignorance of Parliament and the English not to see the illu- sion, the deception, and the hypocrisy—not to see, in fact, that it is the old body of the grand jury, which is supposed to have been put out at the front door, which is very gracefully admitted again at the back door."
On Monday night a fire broke out in the outdoor de- partment of the Crewe Railway Works, and spreading rapidly, did damage estimating at about £50,000.
LOCAL NEWS.
ACCIDENT AT WESTON QUARRIES.
A man named Harper, of Cawdor-st., Runcorn, employed at Weston Quarries, fell a distance of 35 feet on Thursday whilst engaged in his work and sustained a compound fracture of the ankle joint.
NON-PAYMENT OP WATER CICARGES AT RUNCORN.

On Monday 81 persons were summoned by Runcorn Waterworks Company for non-payment of their water rates. The majority of cases had been settled out of court; in the others the requisite orders were made.
ST. BEDE'S SCHOOL, APPLETON.

div.head: BETHESDA BAND OF HOPE. RUNCORN.
div.p: BETHESDA BAND OF HOPE. RUNCORN.

The last entertainment of the season, under the aus- pices of the above society, was given on Wednesday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. Loony, and there was a crowded attendance. A programme of part songs recitations, dialogues, songs, and duets was rendered in a thoroughly enjoyable manner. The choir are to be congratulated upon the excellent way in which they interpreted the selections. RUNCORNMESLEYAIi CIRCUIT. The quarterly meeting was held on Monday under the presidency of the Rev. Thos. Wilkes, supt. minister. The financial statement showed a balance on the quar- ter's working. There was a slight decrease of members. Unanimous votes of thanks were accorded to the Revs. Thos. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmith, and J. Hanby for their services, and those gentlemen were heartily invited for another year, and the invitation was accepted. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED,—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. SODDEN DEATH OF THE WIDNES POSTMASTER.

Mr. Richard Baxter, of Wellington, Salop, arrived in Widnes n the 23rd March to take charge of the Post- office in succession to Mr. J. Payne, who had resigned, and he took up his quarters at the Central Hotel. Be was suffering from a severe cold at the time, which de- veloped into congestion of the lungs and Drs. Allen and McLennan were called in, but he gradually sank and died on Tuesday night. For some years Mr. Baxter was connected with the Warrington Post-office. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J, and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.— Advt. A HALP-HOLIDAT FOR GROCERS ASSISTANTS AT RUNCORN.

, The grocers' assistants in Runcorn have held a meeting and appointed a deputation to wait upon their em- ployers with the object of prevailing upon them to close their establishments from bne p.m. on Wednesdays on and after May 4th. When it is known that this hard- worked class labour for 78 hours a week, the public will sympathise with their request and aid them in their en- deavour. The deputation consists of Messrs. William- son, Basnett, and Mines.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

Yesterday the voting papers In this contest were dis- tributed. rhey will be collected on Wednesday, and counted on Thursday, and great interest is being mani- fested in the probable results. The addresses of the various candidates may be perused in our advertising columns, and there is quite an army of canvassers at work in the interests of all the gentlemen. Both the retiring members and the Ratepayers' Association are confident of success, and it must be agreed that the issue of the struggle is very doubtful.
TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT WIDNES.

The first course of lessons in technical dressmaking held in Lacey-st. School, under the auspices of the Technical Instruction Committee, has been brought to a close by an exhibition of the work done by those who had attended the classes. The excellence of the fwork done and its varied description was a marked tribute to the teaching of Mrs. Dobson. Three prizes were offered for competition by the pupils, and the first nrize.a beau- tiful handworked tablecloth ,was awarded to Miss Savage, of Higher Runcorn. The classes have been so satisfac- torily attended that they are to be continued. APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS IN RUNCORN DISTRICT. The four Malls arranged in the room were laden with the customary class of articles, and various amusements were provided. The Rev. W. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES NEWSPAPER OFFICE.

Patrick McNicholson, Owen Carlin, Thomas Walsh, John McEavers, Charles Martin, John Johnson, bovs, were brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, charged with breaking into the" Daily Post" Office on Monday night and stealing therefrom £1 19s. the monies of Messrs. Russell and Jeans. Martin and Johnson pleaded not guilty, and the others pleaded guilty. It appeared the boys:had obtained a key which fitted the office door, and on Monday night they obtained an entrance and abstracted the money from the drawer. They were apprehended by P.C. Cochrane on Wednesday night, when they had spent a sovereign of the stolen money.—Martin and lahnson were discharged, and the other prisoners were each ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. DEATH OF Mn. KIRKHAAI OF WESTON.

It is with regret that we record the death of Mr. John Wesley Kirkham, of Weston. For nearly two years Mr. Kirkham had suffered from a chest affection, and some weeks ago he went to Llandudno, in order to obtain the benefits of a change of air, and he died there on Tuesday morning, at the age of 55 years. The deceased gentle- man was the son of Mr. Wesley Kirkham, late manager at Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons' Works, and he served his time as a bricksetter. He was for a long period foreman of Weston Chemical Works, and about seven years ago he was appointed manager, which onerous position he held until his health failed him. In recognition of hia long and faithful service the directors made him a hand- some allowance. In all public matters connected with Weston, Mr. Kirkham took a deep interest, and for a number of years he was one of the Guardians for the township. In religion he was a Wesleyan,and he had held the principal lay offices in connection with the local chapel, and was treasurer of the Day school, until ill- health compelled him to resign. His remains will be interred at Runcorn Cemetery this afternoon. div.head: CRUELTY TO A EtORSE AT WIDNES.
div.p: CRUELTY TO A EtORSE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Cregan, 8, Granville-st., a carter, was summoned for cruel treat- ment of a horse,by working the animal whilst in an unfit state. On the 22nd March,.P.C. Cummings was at Hal- ton-view,and saw the defendant driving a horse attached to a cart of cinders. As the animal appeared in pain, he made an examination and found on tho off' shoulder a wound running matter, and underneath the saddle was a raw red flesh wound, the size of a five-shilling-piece. Some coarse sacking was saturated with matter. The horse was in great pain, and in very poor condition.— The Bench said it was a very bad case, and inflicted a fine of 10s, and costs, 125., or 14 days' hard labour. PlizsExraTiox TO THE REV. J. R. div.head: PRESENTATION TO Ai CHOIR CONDUCTOR AT WIDNES.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO Ai CHOIR CONDUCTOR AT WIDNES.

An interesting gathering took place at Deacon-road Baptist Chapel, on Munday evening. Proceedings com- menced with a tea party, and then followed a concert, an admirable programme being gone through. During an interval Mr. Isaac Edwards was called upon, to his great surprise, to twelve an illuminated address and a silver-mounted baton from the hands of Mr. W. Clarke, of Beaconsfield Masse; The address,,which was suitably framed, read as follows:—" Presented to Mr. Isaac Edwards, with the accompanying baton, by friends in connection with the Widnes Baptist Church, in grateful acknowledgment of valuable services rendered by him for many years past, and especially for the uniform in- terest he has taken in the musics! services of the church, in the earnest hope that, with Csod's blessing, he may still be spared to continue his work for many years to come." Mr. Edwards appropriately acknowledged the unexpected gift.

div.head: MUMMY FEHR LIBRARY COMMITTER.
div.p: MUMMY FEHR LIBRARY COMMITTER.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. T. Sadler. There were also present Dr. O'Heeffe, Messrs. W. Sadler, J. Midwood, D. J. Brookes, J. H. Lee, F. H. Pankhurst, and T. Craik (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian.) Miss Proctor reported that during the past month the total attendaace at the reading room was 13,004. daily aver- age of 520. The books issued number 5,455, an average of 982 in the lending department and 59 in the reference department. The average daily issue was 218. The fifth annual report was also presented, and showed that the Library had been open 307 days aid that the number of visitors was 154,473, an increase on the previous year of 13 per day. 487 volumes had been added to the Library, 483 by purchase and four by gift. The number of volumes in the Library was now 4,979. 53,901 volumes have been issued during the year for home reading, and 1,734 had been consulted in the reading-room, being a daily average of 181, increase 7 per day. There were 2,982 borrowers on the register.—The reports were adopted.—On the proposition of Mr. Pankhurst,seconded by Mr. Lee, and supported by Messrs. Brookes and Dr. O'Keeffe, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman (Mr. H. Wade Deacon), for his services dur- ing the past year. Mr. Deacon was described as a model Chairman, and hearty sympathy with him in his illness was expressed. UMBRKLLIS RECOTERED.—J. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. RAILWAY COLLISION NEAR ATHERTON.

On Wednesday night a collision occurred between passenger and coal trains on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway at Peelwood Siding, Atherton. It appears that a coal train was being shunted across the metals when the half-past seven passenger train from Wigan, containing about a dozen passengers, I ran into the coal waggons, causing great confusion. Several of the waggons were knocked off the metals I smashed, and the coal scattered about the perma- nent way. The engine of the passenger train met the full force of the collision, and was much dam- aged in the front portion, although the speed had been greatly reduced by the driver. However, along with the carriages, it kept on the rails. Several of the passengers opened the doors and jumped from the train, thereby receiving slight injuries. Little or no injury occurred from the collision itself. The line was not damaged, but it was not cleared be- fore one o'clock on Thursday. Mr. Brighousei the c.o.r-o-n—er--, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Accident Hospital, on the body of Thomas Murphy, aged 42, of g, Eleanor-8% who was killed at Hutchinson's chemical works, on Satur- day. The deceased was foreman of the caustic de- partment, and he was stan4ing on a wooden stage in connection with the revolving pans,superintend- ing the removal of some bricks, when one of the planks gave way and he fell to the ground a dis- tance of 12 feet. Dr. Hudson was called in and found that his collar bone was injured, and several ribs fractured, the bones penetrating the lungs. He was removed V. the hospital, where he died in a few hours, his case being hopeless from the first' The evidence showed that the planks were resting on stout iron bars, and as there was no appearance of neglect a verdict of " Accidental Death " was recorded.

A DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN, Mr. Worsley, coroner for the honour and foe of Halton, on Thursday held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of Catherine Hassey,aged 56, of 24, Cooper-st., wife of Martin Hassey, shoe- maker. It appeared that the woman left home about seven o'clock on Sunday night, with the intention, it was understood, of going to a neighbour's house, and she was not again seen alive. About 9.3 Q p.m., Wm. Plant, of Prescot Terrace, was passing Delph Bridge, when he saw the body of a woman lying in the water. He attempted to recover the body, but failed, and he called P.C. Woolley and a Constable to his aid, and together they brought the body to the bank. Life was quite extinct. The clothes was tucked up to the woman's waist,and these had kept the body afloat, while the head and legs were im- mersed. As the woman was not recognised,she was taken to the Mortuary on the police ambulance,but her husband identified her on Monday, and she was removed to her home.—As therewas no evidence to show how deceased got into the water, a verdict of "Found dead" wee returned,

div.head: WIDNES SOUTH COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES SOUTH COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION.

The question as to who shall fill the vacancy on the Lancashire County Council, created by the elevation of Mr. Snape to the Aldermanic Bench, will be decided to-day at the ballot box. The poll- ing booths are at the National Schools,in Waterloo- road, and the number of voters is about 2,400. On Thursday night a public meeting was held in the Baths Assembly Room in in support of the candidature of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candidate, and there was a large audience of electors. Mr. T. Sutton Timmie presided and in advocating the claims of Mr. Deacon, drew attention to the valnable public work he had done on the various local bodies, and to the noble philanthropy associated with his issue, and said that it would be downright ingratitude if they did not elect Mr. Deacon by a thumping majority. (Applause.) As to Mr. Sayce let him serve an apprenticeship on their local bodies before as- piring to be a full blown County Councillor. (*Laughter and applause.) Ald. Snape proposed the resolution of confidence in Mr. Deacon, whom he described as a gentleman peculiarly fitted by his training and ability to deal with the important questions that came before the Council. (Applause.) Mr. Rescose seconded the 'notion, which was supported by Mr. Bancroft Cook, of Liver- pool, and carried unanimously. Mr. Deacon was un- able to be present through illness.—A meeting in support of Mr. G. Sayce, the Conservative candidate, was held in West Bank Mission Room on Thursday night, and there was a good attendance. Mr. James White pre- sided, and Mr. Sayce made a speech, and a resolution of support was carried unanimously.
Mr. Joseph Austin Chamberlain was on Wednesday elected successor to Mr. Hastings in the Parliamentary representation of East Worcestershire without opposi- tion.

Sir George Trevelyan, addressing a great demonstra- tion at Wigan in support of the two local Labour candid- ates on Wednesday night, said never had Mr. Gladstone shown a more noble average of speaking power than during the present session.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

That—Y;ra-s--a curious and unusual incident that occurred at Runcorn Musical Society's concert on Monday, but the audience as a whole were indul- gent, and prepared to make the best of a bad thing. It was certainly a most cogent example of "Ham- let " with the part of Hamlet left out, but after all the concert was highly enjoyable, and previous disappointment was forgotten. when the powerful and musical tones of Mr. Pierpoint were heard ring- ing through the Hall. He was in exceptionally fine form, and Runcornians are proud to claim one who has climbed so high up the ladder of musical fame as a native. It should be clearly understood that no blame attaches to Mr. Pierpoint for Mon- day's mistake. Had he not been on his way to ful- fil his engagement for Tuesday, as he supposed, he could not have been present at the ccucert at all, and bad would have been made much worse. I have heard one or two persons state 'that they would not again subscribe to the Society, because of this mishap, but it is to be hoped that no gentleman will be so unreasonable and so deaf to the grand record of the Society as to carry out such a course. A similar occurrence may easily be avoided in future by giving the artistes notice of their engage- ment about a week before it should be fulfilled.

The extraordinary election of a CountyCouncillor for Widnes South does not appear to be arousing much enthusiasm. It is generally believed that there is only one in it, and that is not Mr.Sayce,but it will not be wise for the Liberals on that account to be in any way lax in their eff irts. Every avail- able vote must he polled so that Mr. Deacon may be returned by such a majority as to show the strength of the party, and the uselessness a contesting the seat at any future time. It is unfortunate that Mr. Deacon should have been attacked by the inftuenza at such a time, and the sympathy of all is extended to him with the wish that he may be speedily tak- ing his usual active part in the affairs of the town. Mr. Deacon's absence ought to make his supporters work all the harder to secure his victory, and I am pleased to see that the newly-formed Women's Libe- ral Association have already got themselves into fighting trim. They are training for the General Election by canvassing briskly for Mr. Deacon on the present occasion.

An election for Guardians at Widnes has been avoided, and I am sure that the rateyayers will not be sorry to have this removed from their path, 80 that they can give more attention to the County Council and Local Board elections. There were ten gentlemen nominated for the four seats allotted at Prescot Board of Guardians to Widnes, and these candidates had a meeting on Thursday and arranged that Dean Finegan, Major Wareing, and Mr. George Davies should be again returned,and that Nir.Randle should take the place of Mr. Peover.

The Widnes Local Board Election on the present occasion promises to be of a very keen and excit- ing description. The Ratepayers' Association are determined to demonstrate, and have the promise of the popular vote at their back, and the retiring members are equally working to retain the confid- ence which the ratepayers have reposed in them in the past. Then there is one candidate who is the nominee ot the Irish National League, and Mr. Bronchemite is" a man of himself" and has even issued a weekly sheet which he calls " The Lanca- shire Telephone "to advocate his claims. It would be a difficult matter to make a forecast of the re- sult, The choice is that of the ratepayers, and it is to be hoped that it will be a wise one.

The Pontypridd Local Board contemplate carrying out a subsidiary drainage scheme for the district, and in response to their advertisement 17 tenders have been sent in for the work. Amongst the list of contractors appears the name of the firm of Messrs. Weston and Woolley, of Runcorn,who under- take to carry out the scheme for .£19,810 us. Id. The highes•:, tender is that of Messrs. Thomas Evans, Cardiff, .£39,870 and the lowest that of Mr. T. Jones Davies, Cardiff, £15,599 19. 9d. Success to the Runcorn firm !

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The last concert of the fourth season of Runcorn Musical Society was held on Monday evening i the Public Hall, and the very numerous audience that assembled was an unmistakeable evidence of appreciation of the efforts of the society to provide music of the best and highest class. The work chosen for exposition was Haydn's " Creation," aria, it is not an exaggeration to say that but for an un- fortunate mishap in the arrangements, the performance would have equalled, if it did not surpass, any of the previous efforts of the society. The principals engaged were Madame Conway, Mr. Maldwyn Humphreys, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint,but Mr. Pierpoint failed to put in an appearance at the appointed time, and the concert ' had to proceed without any representative of Raphael and Adam. It transpired that when the season's pro- gramme was arranged, this concert was fixed for the 29th, and Mr. Pierpoint had been engaged for that chit-, and no intimation of the alteration was conveyed to him; hence his non-appearance. He was, however, on i his way from London at the time, and in order that he might be present in the evening the band lengthened out the programme by the performance of the selections Zampa and Carmen, which were much enjoyed. The choir was not at its usual numerical strength, only numbering about 70, but the several parts were *ell balanced, and the choruses were sung with a power and a finish that was gratifying to all con- cerned, and the audience frequently showed their opheion by prolonged applause. Madame Conway was alloted the parts of Gabriel and Eve, and she scored an unqualified success. Her rich and pure voice was heard to great advantage, and she had to ac- knowledge encores on more than one occasion. Mr. Waldwyn Humphreys (Uriel), is the possessor of a tenor voice of admirable quality and power, and his rendering of the various recitations and airs was a rich musical treat which his auditors were not tardy in acknowledg- ing. Of course the base parts were practically left out, I and Haydn's great work was, therefore, heard under circumstances which prevented a just appreciation of Its beauty. Mr. Pierpoint arrived in time to take his share of the third part of the programme, and this he did in a manner which enhanced his reputation. Con- i sidering that he had just completed a wearisome journey, and had hurried to the Hall; his performance was very fine. As some amends for the disappointment caused by his late appearance, he sang two of the principal solos in the first and second parts, and ho received an enthusi- astic encore for "Let the earth bring forth." The accompaniments in the creation are a striking feature, I and add much to the beauty and dignity of the work,and I the band, under the leadership of Mr. J. W. Collinson, I gave a most skilful and powerful interpretation of the score. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the hon. conductor, displayed his customary ability in wielding the baton.

div.p: PENKETII
THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

On Sunday, in connection with the above chapel, two addresses were given in the Sunday School, morning and afternoon, by the Rev. Gnanamutthu J. Israel. In the morning the Rev. G. .1. Israel gave a short andress to the children, and in the afternoon addressed the school and friends relative to child marriages in India, and the position the female portion of the community occupy, and the way in which they are treated. In the evening in the chapel the pulpit was occupied by Mr. Israel. There was a large congregation. The text was selected from St. Mark i. 40 and 41. On Monday evening, in the schoolroom, the same gentleman delivered a lecture, entitled "My work amongst the slum children of India," or "The darkest India, and the way out." Mr. 11. Garnett, J.P., occupied the chair, and introduced the lecturer. The lecture was illustrated by a number of ladies and gentle- men dressed in Indian costume. The lecturer said he was a 'Endo() christian missionary of the Wes- leyan Methodist Missionary Somety,and was work- ing amongst the poor children of India. Several questions were afterwards asked bty several of the audience, and were satisfactorily replied to. The total of the collections taken amounted to .£6 12s. lOid. The meeting, which was a crowded one ter- minated after singing the Doxology.

div.head: FRODSLIAM,
div.p: FRODSLIAM,

IFUNERAL OF Miss. REYNOLDS.-011 Wednesday. the remains of Mrs. Sarah Florence Reynolds, wife of the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, Vicar of Kingsley, were laid to rest in a new grave, within a few feet of the entrance to Kingsley Parish Church, amid manifestations of sorrow. AGRICULTURAL Lam:ram—On Tuesday evening a lecture, under the auspices of the County Council Tech:Aral Instruction Committee, was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, by Mr. Roberts, entitled "Clover And Root Crop Cultivation." The Chair WM OCCIIPied by Mr. Thomas Baxter, C.C.,_of Dutton Hall. CHURCH Or ENGLAND MISSIONARY SOCIRTY.—The r annual meeting of the Frodsham branch of this society , was heid in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday even ing, the Rev. EL E. Blogg, M. 1., in the chair. Dr. Weaver (treasurer) read the statement of accounts, which showed that the past year amounted to £5B 4. 31., less expenses £1 Os. 61. Dr. Weaver stated that as himself and family would be leaving the locality shortly, Mr. Carpenter had kindly consented to become treasurer in his stead, and in all probability Miss Wright would be collector in the place of Miss Weaver.—The Chairman spoke of the loss they would sustain by the removal of Dr. Weaver and family from Frodsham, and urged the claims of the Church Missionary Society. The deputation, Rev. Mr. Dixon, attended, and gave a very graphic and interest- ing account of the origin and work of the society in Uganda, on the east coast of Africa. The OVREISRICRSHIP DISPUTIL—At the Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. A. Fletcher of Northwich, ap- plied for the appointment of Mr. Edwards, of Frodsham, as one of the overseers for Frodsham township. Be said that Mr. Edwards had been nominated with two others, Jou Ruth well and Thomas Davies, and the reason Mr. Edwards wished to be put on the list of overseers was that he thought the overseers should have a banking account, and he, for one, would carry out that proposal If appointed.—The Chairman did not think that the ap- pointment of three overseers was advisable, and read a petition, which the magistrates had received from some of the ratepayers of Frodsham. asking them to appoint Messrs. Davies and Rothwell. He considered these two gentlemen were efficient enough to fulfil the duties of the office. He had no doubt that they would start a banking account.—Mr. Fletcher: That's all Mr. Ed wards requires. If they will do that he will withdraw.—The Chairman (to Mr. Edwards) : I understand that you have not paid your old rates.—Mr. Edwards: I said I would pay them to Mr. Davies if he would bank the money.— Mr. Fletcher: Mr. Davies is a very old man, and he is becoming infirm, and I think the action that Mr. Ed- wards took was quite justified. The Local Government noard had suggested that a majority should rule, and Lwo was not a majority, and, therefore, he thought that three overseers should be appointed. The magistrates decided to appoint Messrs. Rothwell and Davies as over- seers.—Mr. Fletcher: I am sorry that your worships at- tach so much importance to a memorial. We might have got one in opposition.—The Chairman: We are not led by memorials, for they are so easily got up.

Lord Salisbury is expected to follow the Marchioness to Beaulieu at the end of next week. Ile will be within a short distance of Ilyeres, and may possibly pay a visit to the Quern.
_ Great uneasiness, a Berlin correspondent states, is being felt in Berlin military circles, owing to the con- tinud massing of Russian troops near the German North Eastern frontier.
The girl Edith fife, the supposed mother of the child whose body was found at Southampton in a clothes box, died on Monday night. The girl's friends live at Shipston- on-Stour, Worcestershire. •
THE HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN
WARRINGTON.

A meeting of the committee of the Warrington Shop Assistants' Association was held on Monday evening, when it was repotted that success con- tinued to att nd the movement. It was announced that other tradesmen had consented to close on Thursday afternoons, commencing on April 28th, including Messrs. Melia and Company, Mr. William Gleave (baker), and Mr. F. W. Ilallwood. A sub- scription list has been opened for paying the pre- liminary expenses of advertising, &c., and it was announced that a generous response ha l already been made by the tradesmen of the town. On Thursday afternoon the closing of shops was even more widely observed than in the previous week, and the assistants now feel assured that the movement has been firmly established.
SHOCKING SEQUEL TO A STREET FIGHT.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Thomas Rralinson, of Salkeld-square, was again charged with unlawfully wounding Frederick Pilling, of 11, Sutton-street, on the 12th March.—P.S. Woolley said the injured man had had a relapse, and had now been unconscious for 18 hours, and grave doubts were entertained of his recovery. On the applic..tien of Superintendent Atherton the prisoner was remanded until Monday, bail being refused. At three o'clock on Thursday afternoon Pilling succumbed to his injuries, and this fact caused much excitement in the neighbour.. hood. The deceased, who was 28 years of age, was employed on the Manchester Ship Canal Works, and it is alleged that he and the prisoner had a fight together in Mersey-street during which a scuffle took place on the ground, and the deceased sustained severe injuries to the left side of the head. His depositions have not been taken and it will depend upon the evidence brought before the Coroner as to what charge will be brought against Rawlinson. The Coroner has ordered a post marten examination to be made.

div.head: COMING ELECTION AT WARRING.
div.p: THE COMING ELECTION AT WARRING.
TON. LIBERAL RECEPTION MEETINGS.

The Warrington Liberal Association have arrang- ed to hold another series of reception meetings on behalf of the Liberal candidate, Dr. Arthur Houston Q.C., similar to those which proved eminently suc- cessful and evoked so great enthusiasm a te a week ago. Beginning on Monday next, a meeting will be held every night throughout the week, and at each of these Dr. Houston and other speakers will deliver addresses, and Mrs. Houston and Miss Daly will take part in the concert which comprises a portion of the programme each evening. Amongst those who in addition to Dr. Houston are expected to address one or other of the meetings are Mr. Theodore Fry, M.P., Mr. A. J. Symonds (National Reform Union), Mr. T. S. Leadam, Rt. Hon. J. Stalls- field, M.P., Mr. J. F. Taylor, (Irish correspondent "Manchester Guardian "), Mr. C. Furness, M.P., and Mr. C. T. P. Wright, M.P., (Dnblin University). On the 13th inst. a mass „meeting of Liberals will be held in the Public Hall, at which Mr. Samuel Walker, Q.C., Mr, Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Dr. Houston, Q.C., will be the principal speakers.

div.head: WARRINGTON FORGERY CASE AT THE ASSIZES.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON FORGERY CASE AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge presiding, Thomas Edward Baines (34), clerk, pleaded not guilty to forging a certain accountable receipt for .f.:2 ss. at Warrington, on New Year's Day, with intent to defraud William Johnson.

- -----___. Mr. Foard, who prosecuted, said prisoner and Hill, the prosecutor, were friends, and the latter asked him to engage the Warrington Concert Hall for a certain date in order that a concert might be given on that date. He gave prisoner £2 ss. with which to pay Johnson, the secretary for the hall, and prisoner afterwards returned Hill a receipt for the money, which purported to be sighed by Johnson. The money had not been handed to Johnson, and Hill, hearing of this, had prisoner appre-

Mr. Segar, for the defence, pleaded for leniency, and contended the signature was not made with the inten- tion of defrauding Johnson. Prisoner put the money in his pocket for the time, and wrote the receipt as a matter of convenience.
His lordship instructed the jury that there was prac- tically no defence. The jury found the prisoner guilty. and he was sentenced to four months' hard labour.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THEFT or NEWSPAPERS.-At the Newton Petty Ses- sions on Saturday, Brian Flaherty, a new corner from Ireland, was charged with stealing on the 19th inst., a parcel containing 23 newspapers value is. 11d, the property of W. H. Smith and Son, from Chester railway station.—Thomas Henry Guest, a boy employed by Messrs. Smith, deposed to putting the parcel down near the bookstall and presently missing it.—Wm. Thomas Jackson, porter at Newton Station, said he saw tho prisoner on the platform there on the morning of the 19th of March with a parcel of newspapers.—John Taberner, stationmaster at Newton, said he seized the complainant and took the bundle from him.—P.C. Cameron said on apprehending the prisoner he told him be did not steal the papers but picked them up.—He made a most voluble defence in piteous tones saying he had picked them up in the street. He had come to Eng- land to work for a farmer arid was a strangor in the country.—Fle had been in custody eight days, and was ordered to come up for judgment when called upon.

CHARGE OF THEFT AT THZ BARRACKS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day morning, before Councillor James Fairclough (chair- man), Alderman Wright, and Mr. E. M. Crosfield, John IGlennan, a militiaman, was charged with stealing on March 25th, two blankets the property of the military authorities at the barracks.—Sergeants Craythorne and Jagger, of the barracks proved the case, and the former deposed to meeting the prisoner with the blankets in his possession and "in drink but not drunk." There had been a bedding inspection and the company the man belonged to were 14 blankets short, and it was supposed the pri- soner was taking them for men in that company. He could not satisfactorily account for the possession of them.— The prisoner's defence was that lie was taking the blankets to, the guard room to a friend who had just enlisted, and who he supposed might be there, and would require them.—The Chairman said the magis- trates seemed to look upon the matter more as a breach of discipline than theft, and that he ought to be punished by the military authorities; but after some consideration they fined him 10s. and costs. THEFT OF LIME BY AN IRONWORKER. At the Warrington borough police court en Thursday morning, Henry Miller, ironworker, of No. 2, Hale-street off Longford-street, was charged with stealing on March 30th, a quantity of lime value is. 6d., the property of John Caradise, builder, of DA Burton Terrace, Long- ford-street.—Chief Constable Hunt said the complainant was building some houses in Longford-street, and on Wednesday morning found that somebody had been conveying lime away since the night before. He in- formed the police and P.C. Turner traced the lime to too prisoner's back door. According to what could be seen he had made four journeys. The lime was found upon the prisoner's premises.—Mr. Caradise gave evi- dence as to missing the lime and said he had from time to time also missed mortar and timber. He had no doubt that bricks too had disappeared. He was build- ing nine houses in Longford-street, and expected to build 21 altogether.—Captain Ridgway remarked that there were constant complaints by builders of things being stolen.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 10s. including costs.

LET OFF EASILY. An unkempt looking man named William Dale, who said he was a labourer, but whose hands were declared by the police to be so soft as to show that he had not done much work for a long time past, was charged at Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday with having stolen two pieces of old iron, the property of Dr. Gornall, from Friars-green. P.S. Monaghan said he met Dale in Buttermarket-street carrying the iron and, after asking him a few questions, he found that it had been picked up on Friars-green. Monaghan added that the prisoner told him he had served nine months in gaol for breaking shop windows to the value of V 3, and that he had also been convicted of robbing a child. The prisoner himself did not scent to be much concerned about his position, and he answered the questions of the magistrates in a rather defiant and off-handed manner. When he was asked whether be would be tried at that court or sent to the sessions he said it didn't much matter, and when it was pointed out to him that a man like him could earn sufficient money to live upon, he replied that there were some people who had made a fortune but who did not wish other people to make one. In the end the magis- trates decided to record a conviction against him, but to let him have his liberty, as he promised to leave the town.

MR. DIGOLE AND THE DEPOTS AGAIN. At the close of the ordinary police business at War- rington on Monday, Mr. Diggle again appeared before the magistrates, and complained that the smell as to which he had previously had interviews with the Bench, continued, and said he had prepared a plan which if adopted would obviate the nuisance. He was prepared to carry it cut at his own expense.—Aldeiman Francomb : We understand you have a patent van to cure the smell.—Mr. Digale : Yes—Aid. Francotnb : There would be no nuisance in the street if this was adopted ?—Mr. niggle • I think not; that is my impres- sion.—The Mayor: You had better see Alderman Bur- gess.—Mr. Dig,gle : Oh, I might as well see a dummy. (Laughter.) Alderman Burgess won't allow me to go through the depots, but says I must apply to the Cor- poration.—Alderman Francomb expressed the opinion that if Mr. Dig,gle could invest such a van as he said, Alderman Burgess would be only to pleased to adopt it. —Mr. niggle thought if he could have a conference with the managers of the works something might be done to improve the depots and also Longford works; and asked if he might be allowed the privilege of giving a lecture in the Museum Lecture Hall —The Mayor: Well, I will consider about it.—Mr. Diggle : Thank you, gentlemen.

ALLEGED-THEFT OF A RING AND A HANDKERCHIEF. At Daresbury petty sessions, on Tuesday Sarah A. Evans, married woman, was charged with stealing on March 7th, a gold ring, and a silk handkerchief, the pro- perty of John Rawcliffe. Mr. A. Browne defended. The prosecutor said on the date in question he was lodging with the prisoner at No. 2, Chester-road, Wilderspool, and missed the articles, which he had left ' in the pockets of some cl•idles ; and informed the police. He authorised no one to pledge them. He had been to a pawn shop at Warrington with the prisoner, and she had some baby clothes but he did not see her pawn the ring and handkerchief. She redeemed them, and he got his articles back. The police apprehended her, but not at his request. He admitted to Mr. Browne that he had said that if that gentleman would stand aside he would not prosecute.—Daniel Houghton pawnbroker, of Warrington,said the prisoner pawned tile articles with him. He would not swear she did not say they were her lodger's. Afterwards the police came and warned him about them. An hour after the prisoner came to redeem them, but he would not let her have them. The following day the prosecutor came with her and asked him to let her have them, and he did so. She had some baby clothes with her then.—A constable deposed that Rawcliffe declined to prosecute after giving information, but witness apprehended the prisoner and had her charged at the Occasional Court. Rawcliffe told him he had squared it with her.—P.S. Booth corrobor- ated. He said the prosecutor told him and the constable that she had taken the things and pledged them but he had freely forgiven her. —The prosecutor said he hoped their worships would press the case—(laughter)—but they dismissed it:

CHARGE OESTEALING A HEN. At Daresbury Sessions on Tuesday Wm. Worrall, of Latchford, John Rawson, of Grappenhall, John James, and Arthur James, the last-named two defendants being sons of a Grappenhall farmer, were charged with stealing on the night of the 2lith of February, a Minorca hen, the property of Lister Kaye, farmer, near Grappen- hall.—Mr. A. Browne defended.—Frederick Dewitt de- posed that about 10 p.m. on the 28th ult., he saw four men standing 50 yards away, near Mr. Kaye's hen coop, with a dog, and heard one of the men say "Can't you get it," and then they all ran towards Latchford.— Joseph Ashley corroborated.—P.S. Booth and P.S. Millington deposed to apprehending the prisoners the same night. Worrall praduced the hen and said he had bought it from Mr. Kaye's, and that his dog had got hold of it. Witness could see where the dog had had hold of it.—P.S. Millington corroborated Sergt. Booth. Ramsey he stated said "they took the fowl; that is right enough," and Rawson said" it's a bad job.—Mr. Kaye deposed to missing the hen, and within the past few months other fowls. He did not think the prisoner had taken the others.—Lewis Jeffs, called by Mr. Bro woe, deposed to seeing a Minorca hen fast in Mr. Kays hedge about 20 minutes past six on the night of the 28th ult.—Two boys frightened it and it released itself, and went in the opposite direction to Mr. Kay's.—Mr. Browne said Rawson's dog seized the hen in the road in the dark and killed it before it could be prevented. The two men James were behind, and knew nothing about this at the time. Worrall took the hen home with the intention of bringing it back in the morning, ascertaining whose it was, and paying for it, but they were all apprehended in the night before there was time to do this.—The Bench considered the case privately for a few minutes, and then the Chairman said they were satisfied the prisoners took the hen, but considering their previous character and respectability, and the indignity they had suffered, which they fully deserved for their lark, they would be discharged.

div.head: laNalt CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: laNalt CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAV.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair) and Mr. Lewis Voisey. CHARGES OF Tszsz.—Patrick Cavanagh was charged with having ;Olen from the shop of Messrs. Freeman, Hardy,, and Willis, 4, Sankey-st., a man's boot, valued at 3s. 6d., on Friday afternoon. The prisoner said that he wished his case to be tried at the next Assizes. Ed. Hobson, manager at the complainant's shop, stated that on Friday afternoon, about four o'slock, he heard a noise outside the shop, and on proceeding there saw three or four boots on the pavement, and the prisoner walking away with a boot under his arm. He followed him, but Constable Wood came up at the same time, and took the prisoner into custody. Constable Wood stated that at a quarter-past four on Friday afternoon he was on duty at Market-gate. He observed the pri- soner stop at complainant's shop, and afterwards snatch at some boots. The prisoner was going away. with one of them, when he (witness) arrested him and took him to the Police Station. In reply to the charge I the prisoner replied, " I did steal the boot wilfully." The Bench committed him to the forthcoming assizes.— Elizaketh Humphries was charged with having stolen, on Friday night, three shirts and a boy's slop from a clothes line in the yard of George Slider, Percy-st. Sergeant Taylor stated that has a result of certain in- formation, he went to the prisoner's house and searched it. He eventually found the articles produced up the chimney. Having been brought to the Police Station and charged with the theft, the prisoner replied, " I took them.' Alderman Burgess said that the prisoner had been in court on the same charge several times be- fore, and the, Bench had decided to send her to prison for a mouth with hard labour. Mosrar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and Alderman Francomb.- DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.—WID. Mulligan, in Tanner's- lane, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Thomas McGuire, a soldierfrom Lancaster, and William McGuire, an ex- soldier, brothers, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on Pinner's Brow about 11.45 on Saturday I night, also with assaulting two military men Sergeant Peter Hunt, and Corporal J. Schofield, from the barracks. The complainants proved the case, the former stating that they were all in a shop together, and on their com- ing out William McGuire struck him, and Schofield, and Thomas joined in pulling witness's sash off and tearing, it to pieces.—Corporal Schofield corroborated.—William McGuire said the Sergeant first struck him with a stick, which Schofield denied.—A private soldier corroborated the complainants.—Thomas McGuire said the sergeant, on account of being a little higher in rank than him challenged him out to fight, and on their coming out said the sergeant struck him with a stick on the top ot the head and cut it.—The constable who arrested the prison- ers said he cut it in falling in Winwick-street while being brought to the station. (Laughter.)—They were fined 10s. and costs each. DRIINIC.—John Towney, drunk in Scotland-road, on Sunday morning, who was found lying against Walker's vaults, was dismissed with a caution.—Abraham Kinder, on Pinner's Brow, on Saturday night. He was throw- ing his bundle about the street, and on F. C. Corlett picking it up and handing it to him threw it at him, then left it on the footpath and went away. He was dismissed with a caution. 14'mm:co.—Wm. Eddlesten, 5, Pinshop Yard, and James Griffin, 93, Tanner's-lane,for fighting in Wlnwick- st., on the night of March 18th, were bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace, and ordered to pay costs. —Ellen Flannigan, fustian cutter, 9, Garner's Brow, and Mary Crozier, her sister, with whom she lived, wife of George Crozier, were charged with fighting on Pinner's Brow' at 20 minutes to one on Sunday morning. P.C. Ammon, who proved the case, said Flannigan was bleeding from the nose and mouth.—They were dismissed on promising not to misconduct, themselves again. Foams DRIVING. —Samuel Holt, 26 Garibaldi-st., was charged with furiously driving a horse in Sankey-st. on the night of the cycle parade.—P.C. Hollingworth,ls, said the defendant's near shaft caught him on the arm and sent him spinning.—The defendant was ordered to pay costs, 115. CHIMNEY ON Flun.—James Coyne, 24 Winwick-road for having his chimney on fire, was fined Is. DRUNK AND REFUSING TO QUlT.—Flerbert Stokes was I charged with being (trunk and refusing to quit the Star Inn, Longford-st. also with assaulting William Corker, the landlord, on &Saturday night. Mr. Cprker said the , defendant charged him with taking two shillings change of his, and, on his denying it, the money being his own, knocked him off the stool. He was drunk in the house two hours previously and would not out.—The barmaid ,Corroborated.-1 constable deposed to ejecting him from the house, and bringing him to the station as he would not go home.—The defendant said the publican was ,drunk, but a witness came forward and denied this, and Alderman Francomb reprimanded him for his false as- sertions against the landlord's character. He was fined 10s. and costs.—Martin Casey, drunk and disorderly on Town Hill, on Sunday night, was fined. OBJECTIONABLE LANGUAGE.—Joseph Harrisondabourer, no address, was charged with using objectionable lan- guage at Bank Quay Station and also with assaulting Wm. Hartley Arthur, the night stationmaster. Mr. Hartley said the defendant on Saturday wanted to cross the line when an engine and coach were coming up and because he prevented him assaulted him and used the language complained of.—A Railway Detective corro- borated, and said the prisoner kicked at him and was very rough. Be was fined 10s. and costs Tunsnaz.—Before Mr..li.„Garnett (in the chair), Alder-
man Wright and Dr. Gornall.

SoHoof. Casss.—The following persons were fined for not having sent their children regularly to school :—Jas. Canlon Is. ; John Flanagan, Is. ; John Heaton, 23. 61. ; John Holloway, 2s. 6(1. Plumpton, 2s. 6d. : Mary Ann Rigby, 24. 6d. ; George Riley, 24. 6d.: James Stockton, is.; W. Taylor as.—An order was issued against John Rooney directing him to send his child to school. D RONK .—Sarah O'Brien, 19th appearance, drunk in Bank-st., the previous morning, was sent to jail for a month. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—CharIes Mills, tailor, of Liverpool, temporarily employed in Warrington, charged with being drunk and disorderly, in Golborne-str., on Wednesday night, was ctismissed with a caution.—John Cunningham, drunk and disorderly in Market-st., the same night, was discharged on promising to leave the town. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman), and Wright, and Dr. Gornall. WIFE ASSAIILT.—WiIIiam Broadhurst, sawyer, 3 Bram- hill-st., was charged with assaulting Alice his wife on March 25th. The coinplainant said he came home drunk about a quarter to 12 at night, and kicked her in the stomach because she would not go to bed.—The defendant said his wife had run him into debt all over; and went into various irrelevant details. He had pro- mised to be teetotal if she would only keep away from her mother.—She denied being in debt to the extent he stated.—He was bound over in the sum of £2O to keep the peace for six months and had to pay the costs, I.os. DRITNIC.—Mary Turner,in Bank-st., the previous night. She was fined 10s, and costs. CRUELTY To A HORSE. —John Hannan, carter, 2, Gar- den Row, was charged by Inspector D9wty, R.5.?.C.A., with cruelly treating a horse by working it in an unfit state on the 22nd of March • and James Horton, baker, Bury-st., was charged witli causing the horse to be worked.—P.S. Chancier deposed to finding the horse drawing a loaded bread van and bleeding from a lame wound, the belly band rubbing against the wound, In- spector Dowty said he examined the horse at Mr. Horton's stables ; and he corroborated as to the wound.—Hannan denied that the horse started out with any wound upon it. A mere abrasion ;cis caused during the day by friction of the harness.—Dr. Gornall said be had had the same difficulty with his herse in the spring, and might have been summoned. Had he been, he would have gone to prison before he would have paid a fine. —lnspector Dowty said he knew horses were subject to these things at this time of the year, but a twonenny or threepenny Strap would have prevented the friction . Dr. Gornall characterised the case as a very trivial one. —Mr. Dowty, in answer to the Bench, said he had told Mr. Hannan that if the harms had not pressed on the

wound there would have been no cruelty.—The Chair- man said with all due respect to Dr. Gornall it was an unfortunate thing that he had made the remark he had •done.—Dr. Gornall said he could not be prevented from expressing his opinion.—Alderman Wright went below to examine the horse which was at the court doer, and on his return the Bench fined Hannan 10s. and costs and Horton the costs, Dr. Gornall dissent- ing.--Hannan said he would rather pay a fine of £2 2s. for the prevention of cruelty to children, and exclaimed: There is one gentleman on the Bench that does not agree with you. He is shaking his head.—Dr. Gornall said the defendant had no occasion to make that remark ; and Aid. Harrison also reprimanded Hannan for doing so.

the team a trifle, but at any point Runcorn's eight were equal to the Salford nine. Houghton was in fine fettle, and the international was far in advance of his rival Mainwarinx. The three-quarters were best represented by Davies and Pendlebury, whilst Faulkner, Riley, and Hampson were a smart trio in a clinking set of forwards who worked with a will, never showing the least signs of falling off in what proved to be an uphill battle. FOOTBALL.—RIN,BY. The victory over Devonshire brought a cloSe to the season of the Lancashire Rugby Union. It has been very satisfactory on the whole, the only cause for tribulation being the reverse experienced at the hands of Yorkshire. This was lost more by ill fortune than bad play, but it was lost all the same. It was the only one 'nit of the seven engagements which made up the card, in which Lancashire failed to score. Thirty-three players have done duty for the County Palatine, and of these only Coop and Cross have donned the jersey on every occasion. The consistently good play of the Leigh man was one of the features of the season, and -this has been rewarded by his selection as full back in the great match of the year.

The competition for the Yorkshire Rugby Cup was ad- vanced another stage, on Saturday, sixteen clubs being left in for the next round. Of course Bradford settled York without over-much exertion, and they ought to do equally well with Cleckheaton in the next ties. Being at home availed Huddersfield nothing, as their colours were lowered by Halifax. The last-named have now to meet Leeds, which should prove a tremendous attractiqn on Saturday next. It was only after extra time had-been requisitioned that Brighouse Rangers knocked out Man- ningham, and all that Wakefield Trinity could do with Ossett was to beat them by a penalty goal to nil. At several of the ties there 'were very big attendances.
ASSOCIATION.

Sunderland have now reached the top of the League, and mean to stop there. They have, however, three matches to play away, and should not make the mistake of holding their opponents too cheaply. The three leaders have a very safe margin to worg upon, and Ac- crington have again qualified for the last four. The table up to the date is : —Goals-, Plyd Won Lost Den For Agst Pts Sunderland 2l . 17 . 4 . 0 . 74 . 31 ,34 Preston North Bad Bolton Wanderers 23 15 ~. 6 ... 2 ... 43 ... 32 ... 32 Aston Villa 23 . 13 . 10 . 0 . 81 . 48 . 26 Bverton Blackburn Rovers 25 10... 9 ... 6 ... 57 ... 5 ... 8 Notts County 23 . 10 . 9 . 4 . 54 . -48 27 Burnley Wham pton Wandre 23.....9 .- 10 ... 4 ... 49 —27 Derby County Accrington West Bromwich Mb 22 5 ... 13 ... 4 ... 35 ... 54 ... 14 Stoke 23 . 4 . 16 . 3 . 34 . 55 . 11 Darwin 2l . 4 . 15 . 2 . 34 . 82 10

That there is little to choose between Burnley and Wolverhampton Wanderers is very evident. Both their League contests have been drawn, and the two trials of strength have only yielded two goals in all. There were some regrettable episodes at Turf Moor on Saturday,and the referee was to be pitied rather than envied. Both sides sinned alike, and the feeling shown by the specta- tors had not a little to do with the outbursts of temper. Notts County had to appear at Bolton without Harry Daft, whose absence naturally crippled the attacking power. The vacancy was filled by a stripling named Widdowson, and he came far short of the international. Notts were unlucky enough to have a penalty goal scored against them in the first half, and they were vanquished by two to nothing. Both Toone and Sutcliffe kept goal faultlessly. Somerville, Hendry, and Jones were almost irreproachable at back, the fitst-named being simply magnificent.

It is seldem that Blackburn Rovers do themselves justice at Derby, but once In a way they were seen at their best, and came off with a draw. This was largely due to the skilful goalkeeping of Arthur, who is almost as good as ever. The Rovers have only one more League Axture to pass through, and as that is their return at Sunderland they are not likely to improve their position, which is net so good as last year.

Some of the players selected to do battle for Wales against Scotland preferred to asiist their clubs, so that a very scratchy team visited Edin'4urgh, and as a conse- quence the Scotchtuen had no difficulty , winning. They will have a harder task when they oppose England to-day (Saturday). Southerners are indignant that Dunn is their only representative, and they have some ground for complaint. Northerners think/a mistake has been made in selecting Dunn, as both he and Holmes are right full backs.

Wilkinson and Samuel Wright. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICENSE.—WiIIiam Gregory Willett, veterinary surgeon, of Stretton, charged with keeping a dog without a license, was dismissed. CHARGE OF ILL-TREATING A Corr.—Richard Shalreshaft, farmer, High Legh, as charged by Inspector Dowry, R.S.P.C.A., with ill-treating a cow, on the night of the 14th of March, at StoOkton Heath. A constable deposed to seeing the defendant driving the cow on the night in question, and to next morning, about seven o'clock, finding it lying in a ditch. There was snow on the ground. Some men came about eleven o'clock, got a horse and dragged the cow out of the ditch. The cow had been there all night, in snow and rain.—lnspector powty said he saw the cow lying in the'ditch about a quarter-past eleven. It was in poor condition and in calf. The 'defendant told him that he had bought the cow for 505., and was taking it home when it dropped down ,and that he could not get a float to bring it away, but gave it 'a gill of whisky at night and another gill in the morning. The cow, according to his admission, had been lying 13 hours in the ditch.—The defendant said he tried his utmost to get a float, but could not, and he had three sacks put on the cow and gave it a gill of whisky and:three gills in the morning. The cow bad calved,and was now doing well, and the calf, too.—The Bench con- sidered the defendant had done all he could for the ani- mal, and dismissed the case.
