Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that rvports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

FRODSHAM T. WIDNES • RANGERS.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday. Score : Frodsham, 2 goals, 5 tries; Widnes Rangers nil. WARRINGTON " " V. BROUGHTON RANGURS.—At Broughton. The match was started by the Rangers, and Taylor made a grand run into the home territory. The ball did not stop here long, as Campbell and Shlre headed a loose rush down the field, only to see Knowles, Higham, Wistall and Barnes retaliate in a similar fashion. Still the home team had the best of some ensuing exchanges, and although Flampson, Bailey, Forster, and Griffiths cleared the impending danger, a strong attack forced Ashurst to touch down. Taylor and Hampson were the means of their side getting a footing in the Broughton quarters which was supplemented by Griffiths and P. Lawless taking the ball to the 25. Here Lally secured possession, and effected a grand run in at the corner flag. The drop out orought no relief to the Ranger:l, and after a spell of kicking, Knowles almost dropped a goal, another minor following a minute later. A free kick by Knowles kept the home team on the defensive, and when Warrington looked certain scorers, Swindells and Shaughnessey dribbled to midfield. Quick passim, by Hampson, Bailey, and Lally forced their opponents back, a grand rush by Taylor, McGuinness, Westall, and Higham carrying the play to the line. Soon after the ball was passed by the half backs to young Lawless, who, evading one or two eager opponents, threw across to his brother, who rounded his men, gaining a fine try. Some beautiful screw kicking by the younger Lawless was wit- nessed, and, then Lally made another of his inimitable runs. Sampson followed with some powerful punts, but nothing further was obtained up to halt-time. Re- suming operations, the venue of the struggle, by a series of rushes with the home forwards, lay .near the centre. Sampeo'n, P. Lawless, and Molyneaux regained the lost advantage, but a bout of passing by ttm Rangers sent the ball to Ashurst, who was too isafe to pass. Eventually, Barnes, Forster, Molyneaux, and Bailey relieved,' a kick by Lawless travelling to neutral territory. Shore was then prominent bye vigorous rush, but Sampsoqand Lally tackled effectively before he became dangerous. The game now got rather rough, but when Lally got away with a beautiful run and pass to Sampson, the aspect was altered. Lawless, Ashurst, and Sampson showed up with some tall kicking, and a pretty display of passing by Hampson Westall, and the brothers Lawless was only rewarded with a minor, and Warrington won by two tries, five minors, to two minors.
WIDNES V. WERNETH.

Played at Widnes, in glorious weather, before 1,000 spectators. Barber started for Widnes 40 minutes, after the advertised time. No return was made, and Lyons ran to their opponents' line, but without result. Widnes who were short of three of their usual team, kept up the pressure, and Forster all but scored after a fine run. After the Widnes defence had had a turn of pressure, the home team once more attacked. Drummond . made a fine attempt to drop a Waal, the ball falling short. A scrimmage took place on the visitors' line, Werneth breaking away, and play settled in the home quarter. The visitors had a fine chance of scoring, but failed to take advantage of the opportunity. Campcell made his mark in a good position, but his kick at goal was a poor one, and Hewitt transferred the play. After a series of scrimmages Widnes rushed the ball over the line, and Peters scored ;no goal, however, resulted. The home-. eters still kept up the pressure, but without any tangible result. The game ended—Widnes, 1 goal, 1 try ; Wer- neth, 1 try.

div.head: SAL-F-914e.--.11
div.p: Played at New Barnes, Salford, On Saturday. The visitors were without Crompton, and H. Cook played for Salford instead of Sudlow. Faulkner kicked off for the visitors, and immediately Salfotd rushed the ball into the Runcorn half. Barratt kicked over the line and Houghton touched down. On dropping out, the home team were again well on the ball, and Houghton saved a smart huh in splendid style. Good • passing between Riley, Hampson, and Davies placed Salford on the de- fensive, but Smart play by Cook relieved to the centre. Houghtonv with along punt, again transferred play to the home 25.: where Banat passed to Miles, but the latter was tackled before he could get away. the visi- tors could not break through the home defence, though several scrimmages were contested within a few yards of the line. Davies got possession, and rounded his op- ponents, but unfortunately lost the ball at a critical moment. Gradually the Salford forwards, by combined play, relieved the pressure, and took the ball to midfield. Abrams passed to May, and the latter raced across the field, but H. Cook over-ran him, and the ball, coming loose, rolled into touch. Eaeles and Cook then broke away to the centre, where Walsh got possession, and made off for the Runcorn goal. On being tackled lie threw to Barratt, and the latter passed to Miles, who rounded the Runcorn backs splendidly, and scored un- der the posts. Manwaring improved the point with a nice kick. Runcorn were now playing only fourteen men, Dolan having retired injured. Score at half-time —Salford, one goal and one minor; Runcorn, nil. Kent restarted, and play settled in mid-field. Subsequently Miles attempted to get away, but Faulkner and Pendle- bury brought him down before he became dangerous. ' Good passing between the Runcorn backs was nullified ! by Davies having his kick charged down, and Miles taking advantage came through his opponents and punted down the. field. Mainwaring made his mark, ' and with a judicious kick into touch gained a little ground for the home team, but• Houghton with one of his long kicks transferred play to the home 25. Manwaring made a sup in returning, and an exciting bit of play was witnessed between a few of the players on the Salford goal line, the ball eventu- ally being made dead. Afterwards the ball was rushed by the Runcorn forwards to the Salford goal line. Anxiously the Runcorn men waited for an opening, but Salford were too good in their defence and slowly beat back the "wearers of the green," and Miles again smartly ran along the tench line to the Runcorn 25. The play became very fast and exciting, each goal being visited in torn, but no addition was made to the score, which at the close was—Salford, one goal (five points) ; Runcorn, nil. That Salford are a vastly improved team since Runcorn first encountered them this season there can be no doubt, and the combination has returned to form in a surprising manner. It was evidently not Runcorn's day out, for they experienced the hardest of luck throughout the encounter. The loss of Dolan in the first few minutes of the game naturally discouraged

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

For the second time this season Warrington have ac- counted for Broughton Rangers, the return engagement at Wilderspool on Saturday resulting in a victory for our local team by a goal and a try to a try. Warrington have had the ill-luck to face the Rangers on both occa- sions with indifferent teams, and such a valuable trio a James and John Bate and Reesom were absent,the main factors of the now all-round excellent combination. Gresty was away from the Rangers' side.

At 3.40 Bandies started towards the pavilion goal, there being between three and four thousand present. Chapman's response was but a faint one, and from the first scrimmage near the half-way flag Berry dribbled away, and Jolley helping the movement, the oval was rushed to the line, where some quick passing among the forwards saw Davies scoring before a minute had elapsed. This sudden success of Warrington was re- lished by the local enthusiasts' and the applause was deafening when Turner landed the difficult goal. With five points to the bad, the visitors re-started, and the kick-off augured well for the Rangers. For a while the defence of BO3COW, Evans, and Potts was severely tested, but the former was in brilliant form, and Nevins, from one pack, got nicely away' but the final essay lacked finish. Jackson and Wheeler had the Rangers on the aggressive once more,but a well manipulated dribble by Ashton, Teare, Randles, and Buckley located play at neutral ground. Boscow tackled grandly, and found touch on one occasion,which gained for his side a matter of thirty yards. Runs by Turner and Nevins were promptly neutralised by Hurst and Hackfin, and Berry tricked Leathley and kicked down te Chapman, who was passed by Teare. Fine play by the Rangers' half- backs was spoiled by a knock-on, and Evans getting the oval near the quarter-flag, Webster fielded splendidly, and when everyone aeticipated a score, Hurst made for his lengthy rival and floored him before five yards had been covered. The garae, however,was going in favour of Warrington, and some brilliant forward play by Jolley, Thorniley, and Buckley, was seconded by passing by Nevins, Berry, Evans, and Potts. The visitors again dribbled out, of danger, and at this point Handles had to retire hurt, owing to a nasty knock. Following this came a brilliant burst of passing by the Broughton backs, and the sequence was wound up by Hacklin making a fine run to the Warring ton quarter-flag, Jolley effecting his ssoppage. Parker- next had a drop"at goal, but it was charged, and War- rington, ruChing down the open, charged Hacklin's I kick, and Teare passing across to Ashton scoring seemed a certainty, but the home skipper slipped when he had only to stick up tc 'score. His pass as taken, but when near the line a pass forward spoiled the chance. A run by Chapman was negatived by Boscow, and then the Warringtonians had another spell of hard luck, for Nevins, Evans, and Potts passing finely, the latter got over the line, but lost possession when in the act of grounding, and only a minor was scored. An over- anxiety of Warrington neutralized a fine kick by Web- ster, but Evans reade up for the deficiency with a short run and kick to neutral ground. The Rangers' forwards at length got possession, and rushed down the open at a terrifle rate, and although Boscow was smart in staving off the attack for a while, fine play by Wall caused the game to rage at the Warrington quarter flag. Webster and Evans relieved, whilst Donohue got clear, and punted to Hurst, Potts spoiling the player from making headway. Teare and Thorniley tried to break through with single-handed dribbles,but Hacklin was exception- ally smart, and frustrated all attempts to invade. Free kicks fell to Hacklin, Webster, and Nevins, and from the last-named Turner tried a shot at goal, lout it was a poor essay. Wheeler immediately relieVed, Nevis tackling him well, and although Webster foiled Parker grandly, Wall had the goal apparently at his mercy, but preferred to pass, and several homesters being , handy, the oval was worked out of danger, and the in- terval arrived with the score—Warrington, 1-0-1; Rangers, 0-01. Jackson reatirted, and the visitors soon presented a , bold front, Wheeler dribbling through the thick of his opponents, and forcing Webster to kick dead in the first 'Yew moments of play. Turner's drop out saw the Warringtoniins paving a flying visit to the railway goal, and two possible chances of scoring were badly manipu- lated. Parker changed the venue with a tricky run;but Evans, who had not been receiving his fair share of ,work, accounted for the Rangers' return to their quart- ere. , Warrington was again penalized, but Boscow again asserted himself, and another fine kick nega- tived one by Hacklin. Turner now rushed through- and gained an advantage of ten yards, and after this I came a sequence of passes by Turner, Potts, and Nevins, I play being in close proximity to the Rangers' goal line. Berry was penalized, but the kick availed the Brough- ton men little, for Boseow, with his usual judgment, gained the lost ground, and the game was contested at half-way. The home custodian was forced to save a I minute later. A dribble by Fitton, Shaw, and Jackson, taxed Webster's defensive powers, but the homester managed to clear, and then Chapman had a shot at goal, and Boscow allowed the ball to roll dead. The game was going against Warrington at this point, but an en- couraging shout from the onlookers seemed to have an affect, ter a run by Davies was followed by some pro- minent play by Webster. Hurst was responsible again for the game being again on the home lines but this time Turner came through and dribbled to the Rangers' quarter flag. Ashton tipping the oval into touch. From the throw out Jolley got clear, and running finely gained a try, whicn Turner failed to augment. The last few minutes of the game were in favour of the Rangers, and a misunderstanding between the home backs resulted in a score for the visitors near the corner, and the place kick failing, the game terminated. Score :—Warring- toh, 1-1-1— ; Broughton Rangers, 0-1-3. Teame Boscow. back; C. Potts, J. W. Evans, and EL Webster, three-quarter backs; W. Nevins, and J. Berry, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Handles; T. Donohue, H. Teare, J.. T. Thorniley, T. Davies, and .W. Buckley, forwards. Broughton Ran- gers: Hacklin,, back; Hurst, Chapman., and Parker, three-quarter backs; Wall and Loathley, half backs; Jackson, Medley, Mann, Fitton, Shaw, Thomas, Whee- ler, Cleminson, .and Morrell, forwards. Referee, Mr. Hugh Hughes, Runcorn.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

• LYM/4 V. WARRINGTON ST. ELPIIIN'S.—At LyRIM, on Saturday. A good crowd of spectators turned up to witness the last match of the season. Both clubs were Well represented. A fast though rather one-sided game ended—Lymm, 8 goals ; St. Elphin's, 1 goal. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCRoOL V. ARNOLD FIOUSE, CIIRSTER.—ThiS match was played at Chester on Satur- day. div.head: TAMWORTH. RAILWAY OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE TAMWORTH. RAILWAY OUTRAGE.
SENTENCE ON GOODALL.

At the Stafford Assizes, on Tuesday, John Goodall, the local preacher Who was found guilty on Saturday of as- saulting a Mrs. Siddalls in a railway carriage near Tam- worth, was sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard labour. Mr. Justice Hawkins expressed himself as satisfied with the verdict, and remarked that the pris- oner was a most accomplished hypocrite in so conceal- ing his real character. It wilt be recollected that at the time the outrage was committed Goodall was on his way to carry out an evangelising mission, and had in his possession a bag full of sermons. Mrs. Siddalls was so injured by her fall from the train in escaping the criminal's violence that for some time her life was despaired of.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE IN LONDON.

THREE LIVES LOST. A disastrous fire broke out at three o'clOck on Tuesday morning at a restaurant in Victoria-st. Westminster, occupied by Mr. G. C. Done. The lire, which commenced in the shop, spread upwards with alarming rapidity,and before the fire escape could be sent for, two people ap- peared at the upper windows in the midst of the flames and smoke, and alter appealing piteously for help threw themselves to the ground. One was a man and the other a woman. Both appeared to be about thirty years of age. They were frightfully injured, and the man died soon after removal to the hospital. The firemen found the body of a woman, aged about thirty. She had evi- dently been suffocated. The names of the people who jumped out of the window are Martinis. la Franchini and Agostino,Lozzari, both of whom are now dead. The woman found suffocated was a Mrs. Hughes, who was employed in the house as a nurse. The police also found a coffin containing the body of Laurel O'Done, aged fourteen months. who tiled a few days ago. The origin of the fire is unknown.

div.p: MIS6ELLANEOI7S.
The ten-mile Amateur Champanionskip Footrace of England, run atStamford Bridge Ground on Saturday, was won by Sydney Thomas (Kildare Harriers) in .53 min. 21. secs.

A telegram from Melbourne says Lord Sheffield pro- poses to get together the strongest possible English cric- keting team, including Shrewsbury and Gunn, and to take them out to Australia at the end of the present year with, the view of playing three test matches against representative Australian elevens. It is proposed to play the first match of the series at Adelaide in December,and the remaining two at Melbourne and Sydney later on, Lord Sheffield will accompany the home team, as he is an xiaus to avoid the English winter. Dr. W. G. Grace has declined to form one the new English team. Lord Sheffield has asked the Cricket Council to keep the mat- ter open till May, and it is expected that to this the Council will agree.

div.head: NEW ARCHBISHOP OF WEST-
div.p: THE NEW ARCHBISHOP OF WEST-
MINSTER. APPOINTMENT OF DR. VAUGHAN.

A Rome correspondent says that at Tuesday's meeting of the Congregation of the Propaganda the discussion of Dr. Vaughan's letter, in which he stated that he would prefer to remain at Salford ; as he believed he could be more useful there than in London, was very animated, and after the subject had been thoroughly threshed out the Congregation came to the conclusion that •Dr. Vaughan should be appointed. On the decision being con- veyed to the Pope,his Holiness said," I am delighted with the result, which fully accords with my own wishes. Dr. Vaughan will worthily fill the position." The selec- tion of Dr. Vaughan will without delay be ratified by the Pope. The new Archbishop will then go to Rome. The Vatican is quite convincedathat the selection of Dr. Vaughan will be acceptable to the British Government and to English Catholice.
THE VYRNWY TUNNEL COMPLETION.

CELEBRATION MEETING BY THE WORKMEN. , For once the habitual dreariness of Cuerdley Marsh gave way to mirth and jollity when, on Saturday even- ing, some forty of the workmen at the Vyrnwy Tunnel Works assembled at the Ferry Inn, Fidler's Ferry, to celebrate the completion of that all-important water- course, and to do honour to Mg. William Harlow, mana- ger for Messrs. .1. Cochrane & Sons, contractors, who has performed, perhaps, the mlst practical part in the construction of the tunnel. Mr. Barlow, who has been in Messrs. Cochrane's service for about fifteen years, has been present almost constantly night and day at the I Fidler's Ferry works since his firm took over the contract. Mr. T. Arthur King, the inspector of the works on behalf of the Liverpool Corporation, presided over the gathering, and after the removal of the cloth proposed Mr. Harlow's health in felicitous terms. Many of them had worked with and under Mr. Harlow for along time, and as long as they attended to their duties, they had in him one in whose keeping their interests were perfectly safe. Two years ago last December, Mr. Harlow came to the works, and from that time until now he had werked, thought, and schemed with untiring energy, and his perseverance must have been very satisfactory to Mr. Deacon, the en- gineer, and to Mr. Brightmore, the resident engineer. He had a very pleasant duty to perform an behalf of the officials, the employes, and a few friends, and .that was to present Mr. Harlow with a silver cup as a memento of their esteem. The chairman then presented the cup, which was supplied by Messrs. Eklington, of Liverpool, and on which was the following inscription tastefully inscribed :—" Presented to Mr. William Harlow on the completion of the tunnel of the Vyrnwy Waterworks by the men employed, as a token of their respect and esteem. March 25, 1892." In acknowledging the gift, Mr. Harlow said he was proud of the workmen, proud of the recep- tion they had given him, and proud of the completion of the tunnel. The toast of Mr. Harlow's health was duly honoured. The other toasts of the evening were the healths of Mr. Deacon, Mr. Brightmore, the contractors, the visitors, the Press, and the host and hostess. The connection between the tunnel and the Cheshire shaft is now complete, and for the first time Mr. Brightmore was on Saturday able to dispense with thq boat, and cross from the Cheshire to the Lancashire shore of the river by means of the tunnel.

THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY'S BILL.
The committee of:the house of Lords have decided not to take any further opposed Bills before Easter. The above Bill will, therefore, not be in committee for some time to come.

DANGEROUS PRANK BY BOYS AT RUNCORN. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. Alfred Thomas and Mr. James Handley, six boys named John Fisher, William Watts, Thomas Woods, William Sinnott, Daniel Massey', and George Woodfine, were summoned for having, on the 6th March, unlawfully committed damage upon certain personal property of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, consistieg of two wooden trestles, one saw, one square, one portable blacksmith's forge, the jib of a steam navvy, and a quantity of timber, by causing a certain wagon the on the railway there to come into collision with the same, doing damage to the extent of £3. It appeared that on the Sunday in question the defendants had gained access to the Ship Canal railway, near Runcorn Parish Church, where a number of wagons were at a standstill. They uncoupled one of the wagons and by means of their com- bined strength set it on the move. One boy did place a' "sprag " in the wheel, but it was taken out in order that the wagon might go a little further, and it was then Sent down the incline leading to the quarry at No Man's Land. In this place about a dozen men' were at work repairing some plant, and, fortunately, James Walker, foreman carpenter, who was on the bank above, saw the wagon coming towards them, and he raised an alarm, so that they were enabled to get to a place of safety be- fore the wagon collided witli the plant on which they were engaged, otherwise, said Mr. Newman (Grundy, Kershaw, bif Co.), the solicitor who proaecutedi, it was higifly probable several men would have lost their lives. In order to send the wagon down the incline Massey turned a set of points. There as no evidence against Woods, who was discharged,and the remainder were each ordered to pay costs, 4s. 61. The magistrates expressed regret that the law would not permit them to have the defendants well tfirched for their mischievous , and dangerous conduct. PRESENTATION TO MR. J. R. WALKER.

A presentation was made on Saturday evening at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, to Mr. Joseph R. Walker, who will retire this week from the past Of agent No. 5 district of the Manchester Ship Canal. The chair was occupied by Mr. Griffith Griffiths (who, it is stated will succeed Mr. Walker as agent). Mr. Charles W. Sharrock and Mr. Golightly were in the vice-chairs, and the company included Messrs; Joseph 11. Walker, Thomas Morris, Thomas Hirtles, W. J. C. Snell, G. H. Barnes, Puce Williams. J. A. Ewart, E. Smirk, J. Birch, Leonard W. Barnes, Sadler, J. Griffiths, jun., and about 120 mlfmbers lof the staff and workmen. After dinner, the Chairman proposed the health of the Queen, which was duly hon- oured. The Chairman then, in making the presentation, said it was not necessary for him to eulogise the services which had been rendered by Mr. Walker. Be would leave others to do so, but he would ask him to accept the articles, which consisted of a handsome dressing and• travelling bag, a stationery case, and a spirit case with silver fittings, each article bearing Mr. Walker's initials. (Applause.) He asked the company to drink Mr. Walker's health. (Applause.)—The toast was received with musical honours, after which a song, "Skating at Olympia," was sung by Mr. Snell.—Mr. Walker, who was received with applause, said he had spent many pleasant hours during his connection with the Ship Canal Company, but the . pleasantest recollection would be the kind reception that evening. (Applause.) He thanked them sincerely for the magnificent presents which, had been made to him, although he felt he. had done nothing to deserve them. (Cries of "No, no.") As they knew, he would finish his work on the Canal on Thursday next, being the last day in March, and Mr. Griffiths would take his place. He felt sure that the same respect which had been shown to him would be shown to Mr. Griffiths. He hoped the Ship Canal Company would show their res- pect for Mr. Griffiths in a substantial way. He wished everyone present much success. (Applause.) —Mr. Sharrock proposed "time health of our colleagues on the other sections," coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Ewart, of No. 6 section.—Mr, Ewart regretted that Mr. Price was unable to be present—(hear, hear') but private business stood in the way. The relations between the staffs on the different sections had always been of the best: they had always met in a pleasant manner, although there had been at times a spirit of rivalry. They used to examine the newspapers each week to see which steam navvy had tilled the-greatest number of waggons—(a Voice: " Good old No. 5," and laughter)—but he thought that in that respect theirgood friend Mr. Golightly took the cake. (Laughter and ap- plause.) ' He hoped the same spirit of good feeling would always exist amongst the men. A song was then given by Mr. George Harding. Mr. Ewart proposed the health of the staff and others empleyed on No. 5 section. He remarked that the staff was one of the best on the whele of the canal, and Mr. Walker was very fortunate when he undertook his duties to have such men to assist him. I—Mr. Golightly responded, and remarked that those emploTed on No. 5 Section would have been in a fog sometimes if they had not had a man at the head of affairs like Mr. Walker, of whom none of them could speak too highly. Wherk Mr. Walker had seen them doing their best he had assisted them. They had had 'kind words and rough ones--(laughter)—but the good , qualities had outweighed the bad, Otlo3, and there was, therefore no necessity to grumble.. (Applause.)--Song (encored), "Let me like a soldier fall, ' Mr. Leonard Barnes, and "The Sailor's Grave."---Mr. Golightly; in proposing the health of the chairman, said Mr. Walker had told them that in future Mr. Griffiths would be their chief. He could assure him that all employed on the section would be as pleased to assist him as they had been to assist Mr. Walker. (Applause.) The toast was received with ' musical honours. —The Chairman responded, and said he should endeav- our to deserve all the good things which had been said of him. He had been connected with public works for nearly 40 years, and he had always endeavoured to look upon matters methodically. The name of Walker had been a great one amongst them for many years, and. ever since he could remember the family had been the pioneers of the greateat works that had been carried out in the world. (Applause.) That was a great deal to say, and they needed no further evidence of the ability of the family than that .which had been already afforded. The name of Walker would go down to posterity as the greatest pioneer of public works (Applause )—Song, "So it was" (encored), Mr. Snell —Mr. Sharrock proposed the,. health of the visitors. coupled with the names of Messrs. Morris and Sidles. —This toast was also received with musical honours, after which Mr. Barnes sang "The Old Brigade."—Mr. Morris, in responding, said he was very pleased to be with the workmen of the Ship Canal that evening. He canrke into contact with Mr. Walker shortly after he became connected with the section, and he was then under the impression that he was an extremely mild maw—that butter would not melt in his mouth—(laugh- ter)—but it appeared that when he said "Yes,"- he meant " Yes ' ; and when he said "No," he meant " No." (Applause.) The magnificent testimonial which had been made to Mr. Walker showed that the men had a warm feeling for him. If he had not been as straight as a gun-rod they would not have found it, in their hearts to subscribe, and the genuineness of the presen- tation was shown by the fact that it had not been made to curry favour with Mr.Walker,as in a, few months' time he might be at the antipodes. He could assure them that he should always think well of Mr. Walker. (Applause. ) Mr. Walker having proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Snell, Mr. Baines, and the other vocalists, Mr. Birtlefil also responded to the toast of the visitors, fie observed that he had been connected with the Ship Canal from the first. He had frequently travelled over the different sections in his professional capacity. He had watched the progress which had been made from week to week in that huge Masonry on No. 5 section, and which would last for all time, and speak the name of Walker for many ages. (Applause.)—Mr. Sharrock, in responding to the toast of his health, said his knowledge of Mr. Walker commenced when he came into the district about 4t years ago, and he should always look back with please to to their acquaintance. Mr. Golightly su responded .—Other speeches and songs were given. Y ,OL

On Thursday morning was found in the reservoir at King's Norton, near Birmingham, the body of Amy Bakewell, aged 20 years, a teacher in the employ of the Birmingham School Board, who disappeared on Monday, and who is supposed to have committed suicide.—Last week another young lady teacher of the Birmingham School Board also committed suicide in a pool in one of the public parks of the city. div.p: SELECTED READINGS.
I

Form, WAYS 01? READING. —The yearly issue of lew books by the press of the great European states and of our own country is more than a hundred a day. Those already published who 'lon compute ? I have been asked to give some Practical hints about reading, and I want first to tell you of four persons who stand for four types "ef readers. A very bright lady friend, who might have been anything she chose to be as a scholar in pu:,t.ting said to me the other day, after down a novel of most ephemeral kind, •' 11°W I wish I had not got in "-'s bad habit of Flading nothing but novels and the newsp.pers : 113', now I Can't fix my mind on anything solid !" "ne did not fully realise the truth of what she ; did not see that her character had not ,t_h,e strength, her conversation or her know- edge the founda,tion that it needed. How can live on whip-syllabub and Charlotte Russo 842c1 caramels in preference to roast beef, broiled ••11iolien, or even a boiled dish, is a mystery. The tt4c k of nourishment is evident. The first-named tifina are capital in their place for dessert after the Pod dinner. Then I recall another lady who tt;eoB4l_ vorY many books. With a large library, a ok eluo, a pamphlet society, and a score of wsPaPere, she is usually deeply immersed in iterature. Where does all this knowledge go? tight through her brain, and out into nowhere ! 11.0 definite gain for all those hours. Ask for a oertain fact, a date a name, an anecdote, a quota- LO he is confused, and gracefully changes the ec Reading without reflection is like eating Witnout digestion. Nutrition and growth are errested. Then I remember a good family who Intend to read profitably and be thorough and fcareful. And they select for reading aloud in the B'lll4 a history like Clarendon's five heavy volumes on a comparatively unimportant theme. Callers drop in or father gets tired and falls asleep on the tinge, and Alice tries to teach her Scotch terrier a new trick. You see? Itlasn't sufficient a-oe and interest to hold the attention. The fourth. A gentleman who is proprietor of one of lth° largest and most popular hotels in one of our argest cities must be a busy man. Yet I know ;11°6 a one who is one of the best and most satis- .lnotory talkers that I meet. I said to him one "Y. "Do let me ask you how it is that you find time to be informed on all the news of the day, .1411,c1 ono talk intelligently on new books, &c."He When I was a poor boy, working hard all kind old gentleman used to lend me his New haily after he had read it. One night this 10octirred to me, 'What can I remember of what I 4ve read for the past three weeks? What has 1,." going on in England, in Germany, in France? "Lat new book has been published? What t°Oresq has been made, and in what direction?' Pliting aside my precious papers, I went all lound the cirele—politics, arts, news, literature, 1;e•—till I felt I was certain of some things. I save kept up that habit ever since. What I read, Made mine; and if I can't read a book, I read a DO review of it." Definite knowledge is the key to anceess. One hour each day given to reading in tight way will make a young man or young 647,7,-"Ill.nu well-informed and intelligent.—Kate San.

Sir,—l am requested by my committee to ask you to kindly insert the following explanation with regard to Mr. Bantock Pierpoint's misunderstanding with them, as to the date of last Monday's concert. It appears to have originated through a miscalculation of date at one of the committee meetings last July. Monday having been taken for the 29th instead of the 28th March. Mr. Pierpoint was engaged as for the 29th, and, unfortunately, was not notified when the error was discovered, and it was only on his arrival at the station at half-past nine that he be- came aware of the state of affairs, and at once came down to the hall to do what he could for the best under the circumstances. The committee are extremely sorry for the occurrence,and beg most sincerely to thank those present at the concert for the handsome manner in which they accepted the position.—Yours faithfully, R. W. PIERPOINT, Hon. Sec. Runcorn, March 30th, 1892.

div.head: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY.
div.p: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY.

Sir,—ln a recent issue, under the heading of " Things beard and seen," I noticed a short paragraph touching upon our local Art Gallery, and the proposed acquisition of examples of works of art by Warrington artists. I hope, Mr. Editor, your information is correct, and that our Museum Committee is about to stir themselves and endeavour to obtain a few good examples of local talent. Surely Warrington is not going to be behind the times and neglect her Art Gallery whilst we have such eminent artists living amongst us as " Fildes," " Woods " and" Sheffield," and allow other towns and cities to acquire their best works whilst we are simply looking on. Your suggestion, sir, as to the purchasing of two or three examples in Black and White by George Sheffield, is an admirable one, and well worthy of con- sideration, and I quite aequiesce in your remarks that our worthy townsman who is the proud possessor of a few very fine examples by Sheffield, would be easy to treat with. May I ask what has become of the talked of legacy left by the late Mr. Beamont ? Was not this given to the town for the express purpose of acquiring something la the shape of works of art for the •adornment of our Gallery? A suggestion was made in the Council Cham- ber by one of our members to purchase a few photo- graphs or copies of celebrated works. What an absurd thing to suggest or to do! What merit would either one or the other possess ? Have we not at the present time several copies of celebrated works by " Robson," and who would venture to say they are meritorious as Works of Art? If we have money to spend, it would be better to buy a single example worthy of the name of art than yards of canvas without merit. A good example in 'Black and White "by G. Sheffield would be a valuable addition to our Gallery and would be the forerunner of better things. I hope the matter will not be allowed to drop until something more tangible has been done. It is fortunate to have one individual in the Council who delights and interests himself in the matter, and I trust he may push his ideas a little further as they are steps in the right direction. Apologizing for troubling you,and hoping you can find room for my remarks, I enclose toy card and subscr. myself, A LOVER OF ART. Warrington, March, 1392.

div.head: TORY "FACTS" AND FICTION.
div.p: TORY "FACTS" AND FICTION.

Sir,—l have been amusing myself by reading the re- port of the Tory meeting held at the Warrington Club,on Monday evening, 21st inst. Well might Alderman Fran. comb say "They could not have derived more amuse- ment had they gone to a pantomime!" Quite so ! Al- most as good as Salisbury's circus! Then again "They had heard nothing but facts." Here is a statement about facts, which itself is not a fact. Did the worthy Alder- man Include the remark of his brother Alderman who, somewhat in the sale-room style, talks of its being "all humbug and nonsense, to say that it was the Liberals who gave the working-man his vote." This is one of those half truths which can be stated and used as whole lies. If Alderman Sutton knows anything of political history, and is candid enough to avow it, he must be quite aware that, although it was a semi-Tory Govern- ment passed it, the measure had been agitated for and so made possible by—whom ?—by the Liberals. There has

to be a leng period of agitation kr these reforms before they reach the stage of practical politics. The people really owe this measure, as well as vote by ballot and household suffrage, to the Chartists. But who ever heard of a Chartist being a Tory.? I have heard of Peter- loo,and believe the Tories were not advocating the privi- lege of voting for working-men on that occasion. Now who should have the honour, and advantage if there be any, but they who have borne the heat and burden of the day, in advocating these popular bene- fits? Are the Tories, who " filched the measure and passed it merely as a "good move" after haring been made so by the Liberals, are they the party we have to thank ? Sabreing people who are advocating it, and being constantly found on the wrong side whenever it is discussed, is a funny way of "helping the working man to a vote." The Reform coat is a very bad fit when a Tory tries it on. It wasn't made for him, nor he for it. Still he often tries to disguise himself in it. But the old Adam will peep out somewhere. The ass once tried it on in the same way with the lion's skin. Both "Stupid parties" you know., and both betrayeu by talking. It was the bray that did it. But I forgot. Alderman Francomb says " They had ho wish to deceive people." If this be so these poor unfortunate Tories must blunder into the Reform coat by accident ! And if the people are foolish enough to mistake him for a Reformer that is their fault if his gain. Talking of borrowed plumes : We find large talk. about the Conservatives being the party of perform- ances, not of promises. Here lam with the Alderman— Toryism displays very little promise at the present juncture. And some of their performances in borrowed habiliments are more amusing than edifying. We are told that Tories are now progressing, and progressive. Well, it is about time. My notion of Toryism is that it is political inertia. It never moves unless it is forced —except it be either downward or backward, and either of these it will do readily enough. It is the stupid bear that won't climb without the Liberal pikeli at its rear; but having done so, is not bearish enough to refuse the indiscriminate applause of those who forget that the real motive lay in the pikell and not in the bear. I commend these facts to our realistic alderman for Use at the next Tory meeting. Perhaps the funniest simile was that of Mr. Bottomley's Tory Express ! The idea of a Tory being in a hurry to get forward. But there is, at least, one part of an ex- press train with an exact similitude in the Tory party— the vacnum brake—it is worked by emptiness and stops progress. But here the resemblance ceases, for the Tory Express requires the help of the dirty workers to puff it up— and it keeps the brake always on ! Now, Sir, in all this I see no sign at the dawn of political honesty, at least in Warrington. We Radicals— lam fond of the name, for if there be an abuse to be rooted up I think it best to do it radically and thoroughly —we Radicals I say are not immaculate—we have our own sins and shortcomings to contend with, and I think the Tories might let us have what credit is due to us— cf having initiated and made possible nearly all the reforms of which they are now so meretriciously vain- glorious. Mr. Bottomley accuses Mr. Gladstone of having had five wars in five years. Here again let us give the credit where it is due—to the agitators. Who agitated for these wars? The Tories ! Who made them possible, if not inevitable? The Tories. Who scorns arbitration and prefers the bad arbitrament of the sword ? The Tories! And now,who so uses half-truths as to make them do the mischief of whole ties? The Tories !—Yours ac. JOHN PEERS.

MINERS' WAGES, MINE RENTS, AND MINERAL ROYALTIES. Sir,—" Mining questions are national questions.' England's wealth consists largely in her mines of coal and minerals. Government returns show that 600,000 persons are employed in our coal and metalliferous mines. Mr. Percy thinksthat the capital invested therein almost reaches the sum of £100,000,000, while the iron and steel works will represent another £100,000,000, and an additional 600,000 persons employed. The mining industry lies at the root of the iron and steel, and chemical industries as well as being closely, if not indis- pensably, connected with every other trade. Therefore ' the question of Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties is one of vital importance to English trade. In 1854 England made as much iron as all the rest of the world combined. Even in 1875, near the end of our i brief period of inflation. England made nearly as much iron as the rest of all the other nations, " the exa.;t figures being forty-seven per cent." In 1889, we pre- duced only one third of the total production of pig iron, and still less in 1890—about one fourth pig iron. Of steel in all its branches we produced only one third of the total production. The new English invention of basis steel commenced ten years ago, and 1,500,000 tons annually are now made. We now only make a fifth, other nation taking four tons to our one. Mr. Percy says the Acts beginning in 1872 and ending in 1887 have increased the cost of producing coal to the extent of is. per ton. g CI At a rarliarnent involves increase of cost in working mines. "Something must be done !" and can, and will be done, unless we have become unworthy sons of noble sires. Three hundred years since, when timber became scarce for fuel, coal was substituted, and when, in this generation, iron ore seemed to be getting exhausted, a new system of plant was adopted, and steel was aban- dantly manufactured. And now other nations put other difficulties in our path, and can do so. Why ? Royal rent, Ace., crush us. •6 Existing burdens and suggested remedies." (1) State arrangements for the welfare of the state. (2) The state has abolished purchase in the army. (3) The truck system is abolished. (4) The pas, ing of the Hares and Rabbits Bill, giving to the tenant a right to the ground game on the land he rents. (5) Employers' Liability Act making compensation to work- men compulsory, no matter what contracts an employer may make with his employs. (8) The establishment of a railway commission with power to modify railway charges. (7) And an important item, too, is " Land I Commission "which has ot late made great reduction in agricultural rents. Hence the State must mend or end 'mine royalties. Mr. Moskell Peace, secretary and solici- tor to the Mining Association of Great Britain, says it has been found politic from time to time to mitigate the stringency of beases in favour of the tenant. Mr. Peers's Bill,prepared and introduced in the session of parliament 1 of 1888, but not considered, provided against loss of the enormous sums known as overpaid mine rents. But trade, &c., prevents coal,&e. ,being got during the term of leases. (8) Mr. Peace further shows that "The result of the existing condition of things, so different from what was anticipated when the leases were made, is that in taking coat on which very large sums of money as certain rent have to be paid to the landlord annually, the tenant, while seeking to recoup himself for this payment, will pull every ton of mineral he can out of the mine, and if this royalty is leased from several landlords, he may also be tempted to work the minerals with a view to a payment rather than in a workmanlike manner, and in the softest way." Therefore, follows these (9) four sad results. (a) Markets become glutted with ever-produc- tion. (b) Small, or no profits are reaped by the em- ployers who have sunk their capital in the working of the mine. (c) Small, or starvation wages are paid to the miner. (it) Followed by a terrible increase of acci- dents , loss of human life and limb to the sad-fated miner. (e) While the only persons who have done no- thing, and risked nothing, neither money nor life—the landlords, reap, as stated by Mr. Joseph Hyde, in his letter in the Warrington " Examiner " of March 28th, 1892, an annual profit of about £10,0000,000 from the minerals which were created numberless ages since, and which are now become indispensable to civilised life. The final remedy for this state of things can only be found in some just scheme of lana nationalisation which would go to the very root of the matter. And thus purify the fountain, and the streams thereof must be pure. Simply amending the rents and mineral royalties might do some little to help us in the race of nations, for successfully holding our own place in the commercial world, and must be speedily put in force if we are not to go swiftly down the rapids of ruin. Our successful competitors, the Germans, only pay a fixed royalty upon coal of two per cent, on the profits of the undertaking, but no royalty at all on kali ore. Land owners have no interest in the mines, for all mines belong to the State, to which the two per cent, is paid, thus helping to lessen taxation ; neither have their landlords any power to prevent the minerals on their property being worked, it being held essential to the nation's welfare to have freedom in this respect. Also in France coal and iron ore all belong to the State. The fixed rents are indeed nominal ; simply one halfpenny per acre. Here also the royalty is paidout of the profits, not exceeding five per cent. thereof. Further, on com- paring the difference of mineral royalties at home and abroad, Mr. C. M. Percy states in his able paper on the subject In England mineral royalties affect pig iron on an average 45.81. a ton,plates for shipbuilding 6s. 9d. per ton' and steel rails 53. 6d. a ton. In Germany the mineral royalties are on pig iron Bd. a ton, on plates for shipbuilding is. a ton and on steel rails Eild per ton. So that under this head of mineral royalties England has burdens of ts. 4d. per ton on pig irec, 4s. 4d. per ton on plates for shipbuilding, and 4s. 9d. on steel rails, of which our German competitors know nothing, and 4s. 2d. per ton on pig iron, 45. 7d. per ton on plates for shipbuilding, and four shillings and seven pence per ton on steel rails of which our French rivals know no- thing ; and we have to compete with these nations in the market of the world. It is dangerous to the true inter- est of our nation to allow this state of things to continue, and our landed Tory royalty leeches thus to suck the vitality out of the veins of the nation. America in 1860 did not enake 1,000,000 tons of pig iron. In 1889 our cousins made nearly 7,000,000 tons, an increase of 700 per cent. Twenty years since America made 2,550 tons of steel rails, in 1889 two and a half million tons, outstripping England by a long way. Says Mr. Percy: "In the matter of steel manafacture by our own English basis process, England made in two years combined 623,092. Germany in the same period 11,986,395 tons. Our royalty owners eat up the profits of employers, the wages of our working-men, and cause much loss of life and limb, and largely paralyze English trade. Working-men are almost driven to a state of revolution, which must shortly force needful reforms,
MORE "DISTINGUISEIED " VISITORS.

Among the saloon passengers who landed in Liverpool on Thursday from the Inman line steamer City of New York were Frank P. Slavin and C. W. Mitchell, the famous pugilists. They made no stay in Liverpool, but proceeded to London by the two o'clock train from Lime-st., so that they may be in time to attend Tony Moore's ball on Thursday night. They state that they hurried over from America chiefly to be present at this gathering. They go into training a fortnight hence, the fight between Slavin and Jackson being fixed for th• end of May. A large crowd assembled on the stage to witness the landing, but there was no demonstration.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APREL 2, 1892. BRIAISTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. THE RATES OF WARRINGTON. (MIXED.)

unless speedily conceded. " Prevention is better than cure." If our Tory land owners were wise, and Tory politicians wished to secure the votes of working-men would they not have done something before the end of the present parliament which showed that they had the welfare of masses and the nation deeply at heart ? They always are on the side of the oppressor, nor are the Lioerals too much inclined to do all they can for the vast masses of the toiling nation. End or mend at once Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties. This would help us for a season, at least. Small freeholdings are only a means to an end. (a) Working-men cannot be supposed to have money to spend in purchasing land. (b) Such money would be much better em- ployed in cultivation than in buying of land. (c) But few working-men are able to purchase farms. (d) Working-men alone are the cultivators and re- claimers of the land, and all tha wealth of the nation comes from the soil and the mine, therefore in all justice and fair play, the land belongs to those who toil and make it fruitful. The land is the people's, and ought to be used for the welfare of the nation, not that of land- Ibrds. (e) Farm rents should be paid in proportion of the nature and fruitfulness of the soil, or the man hold- ing land of a poor quality could not live on it or compete in the market with the more fortunate neighbour. (f) Small Fretholders, would thus be tempted to sell their farms, to the money-man and land grabber, hence under such a system no permanent advantage can arise from small freeholds. Therefore that system would work its own ruin, and things soon be as they are at present. (g) All present rightful owners of land should be paid a lair price for the land they hold. All lands belonging to the people ought to be taken and given to the people or State. (h) All rent of land and mines ought to paid to the State for the wel- fare of the State and reduction of taxation. (1) State tenancy is therefore the most likely system to make a happy, contented, and prosperous nation, and should become the law of the realm to save us from the tyranny of landlordism, who are the nation's worst foes. My fellow working-men, ponder well matters of this kind, drink less, think more. Why should the working- men who create by brain and muscle all the wealth of the nation be the poorest in the nation ? We have too long been gulled., robbed, and oppressed by the cunning greedy land grablaers, most of them of the Tory politi- cian class.

INCREASE OF 60. IN .TEE POUND.

Below we give various particulars as to the estimated expenditure of the borough for the com- ing year, which are taken from the agenda of the Town Council meeting to be held on Tuesday next. It will be seen that a proposal is to be made to levy an improvement rate of 13s. in the .£ and a sewers rate of 4. in the .£. The improvement rate is the same amount as was levied last year, but the sewers rnte is an increase of 2d. in the We understand that some explanation of the latter will be found in the fact that last year there was a surplus of cash which, together with the twopenny rate, enabled the Committee to meet their engagements. This year, however,there is a deficit instead of a surplus, and consequently, the Committee have had to increase the rate as stated. Last weak the overseers announced their intention of levying a poor rate of 2s. Zd. in the X, this being an increase of 4d. upon last year. The ratepayers have, therefore, to face a total increase in the rates of 6d. in the .£-4d. on the voor rate and 24 on the sewer ;rate. The full rate of the town this year will be 58...2d. in the .£, in piece of ss. 2d. as last year. It is said that the overseers' rate will be some- what in excess of their requirements, as the call on borough rate account is considerably less than had been anticipated.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT NEWTON.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT NEWTON.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. W. Neille, the Liberal candidate for the Newton division, was hell in the Town Hall, Newton, on Thursday evening. Mr. G. W. Rawlins presided, and he was accompanied on the platform by the candidate, Mr. J. A. Duncan, M.P., for Barrow, Mr. W. Urquhart (Newton), &c. The Chairman said this fight which was coining none knew when, had not been entered into lightly or frivol- ously, or from a desire to fight, but they had entered into it as far as they had gone, because they thought that they ought to fight, and that they ought to win, and further that if they tried as they intended to try, they were sure to win. (Applause.) They had entered it because it seemed to the 3flo that the main issues between Liberals and Tories had now reached an acute stage, one that demanded that, at the next general election, every constituency in the country ought to be tested, and every elector ought to be asked his definite opinion upon those important questions, that affected the well being and happiness of the country. (Applause.) Mr. Neille then preposed the following resolution " That this meeting approves the general policy of Mr. Gladstone, and his colleagues in relation to Horne Rule for Ireland, and domestic legislation for Great Britain, and advocates an appeal to the electors as soon as possible on the ground that the majority in Parliament is no longer in conformity with the will of the people." He said that resolution expressed his .view exactly, and he had much pleasure in proposing it. The township a Newton was one of the old corrupt boroughs, a pocket borough, where votes were bought and sold, but those days were gone by. The question of Home Rule must be the most critical question at the next election, and he could not understand how any Tory could vote against Home Rule for Ireland. The only reason he could find , was because the upper classes did so. If they could find that the upper classes in the past had led them correctly, if they could find that the measures they had advocated in the past were right, there might be some justification to vote as they did. The upper classes did not abolish the Corn Laws, did not give us free trade, and were against the extension of the Franchise. (Hear, hear.) The Local Government Bill for Ireland he stigmatised as a miserable wretched sham. It established county councils, but it set over them a Committee. (A voice" A grand jury "). Aye; a grand jury—(laughter and applause)—to watch the County Councils, like a policeman, and if they did anything which thia joint Committee did not approve of, to have them tried for a new offence which nobody knew the meaning of by a judge who had to interpret this offence according to his own ideas, and then out would go the County Councils, and then they had the tyrannous body appointed by the Lord Lieutenant. He particularised the reforms which he said the Liberal party considered should be brought about, and spoke at length on the land question. He wanted to see land made as easily transferable as any form of property, similar to the mode in operation in Australia, where the majority of the workingmen were owners net only of their own houses, but of the land they are built upon which he thought was one of the greatest possible advantages. The reform of the land laws, and Local Government giv- ing the members of small areas the management of their own affairs, the right to set various Laws in operation, would do more to advance the happiness and contentment of the people of this country. (Applause.) If they wanted to see reforms of this kind carried out, they knew how to get them by voting for the right party, and sending them back into power. (Flear, hear.) He wanted to see payment of members, and also payment of election ex- penses, by the State or the community, as the case may be. They would then be able to get representation of every class in Parliament, and if our domestic legisla- tion was to be directed towards reforms, it was neces- sary they should have every class represented, and it was also necessary that they should have Labour candi- dates. (Applause.) No doubt they would be told that they should not vote for him but for Mr. Legh ; but they should ask the party who told them that if he was in favour of payment of members of Parliament. 'rake this constituency, for instance ; they had dozens of men who would represent them in Parliament most success- fully, but they could not do it, simply because they could not afford the expense. Therefore, if any Tory told them that they ought to support a local man, they must tell him he ought to make it possible _to vote for a local man, by voting for payment of members. (Hear. hear.) He asked them to support the party of progress, whose aim it was to make this country as happy and as prosperous as it was possible for human beings to be. (Applause.) Mr. J. A. Duncan, M.P. for Barrow, in seconding the resolution, said he came down to this division for two I special reasons. He knew that their candidate was a , man to be trusted, and a man who was worth a good deal of trouble to fight for, and a man, if they made him their member, that they would find was worth all the trust they reposed in him. (Hear, hear.) Another reason was, he liked to come down to Lancashire, above all places. What Rossendale and Eccles did, they should be able to do when their opportunity came. They had as good a cause to fight as any of the other places in Lancashire. The County of Lancashire is the one which ought by the nature of things, to be especial y radical. (Applause.) None of them knew how long the general election may be selfishly postponed, but at any rate, the Tories had all at once declared themselves to be the chief friend of the working-men of this country. They would find that Conservative speakers would come down and boast of their beneficial acts, and beneficial promises to the working-men of this country. He asked them to consider that the true principle was not that the working-man of this couutry should give his vote in return for a certain patronage promise, but he should be regarded as a free and equal citizen, whose views were to be discovered, whose wants were to be consid- ered. (Hear, hear.) The question was to be regarded rather in this light, that the tru3 friend cf the working- man in this country was the workingman himself. He was not to be a mere vote giving machine, but was to be regarded simply and solely from the point of view of politics as being an independent citizen, equal in point of citizenship with any other man, however wealthy, in the country. The Conservative party in order that they might successfully gull some of the workingmen in the country, had come, in their latter days, as the result of a death bed repentance, and ;had offered to the country, in return for their support at the next election, such things as free education, allotments acts, Small holdings and a labour commission, but they knew quite well how to measure the Conservative vote in these matters. (Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried unanimously. --A resolution pledging the meeting to secure the return of Mr. Neille to Parliament was passed on the motion of Mr. A. J. Rawlinson seconded by A. Luff man.

div.p: Onybody as is weel up i' grammar 'll know as " ! " meeans " wvll, aw'll be d-astit I" Thad perhaps " is abeawt th' richest word he could be fastened to sich a original idea ; it's one o' th' finest things i' English literature, an' sooner " Verax" starts on " Punch " an' better for booath on 'em. lienery, lad, tho r'ally mon recollect as brass con be put to better uses nor pavin' th' bottom o' th' sea, or chooakin' th' fishes wi ; an' a lot better too. For instance—but no deawt some 'II suggest thersels. Aw'm sure o' one thing an' thad is as " Verax" ne'er knew one payson yet as ordered one or his collectors to pass ony perticuler member o' th' con- gregation simply becose he happens to gad a livin' in a less honest way nor at th' tables at Monte Carlo —an' that's posinble, mind yo! Aw know chaps as is church wardens an deacons as lend drunken men an' wimmim th' price ov a quert on th' clooathes off their back; an' officers as runs a swindlin' raoney-lendin' bizness, ore bogus inshurance com- pany. Wod be thad? Well, these chaps' subscrip- tions isti'd refused varra oft; an' " Verax " mon ha read ce mony a institution as hes bin feawnded an' , aupport4cl NO' brass getten in a woss way nor Peel's getten thad Ave theawsand. Onyway, Doverites doesn'd need to fear a heigh tide through thad five theawsand bein' sap- lied i' th' seaa ; an' iv " Verax " hes heeard fro' Peel wod he eally does intend tcedo th' brass aw hooap he'll let us know. My opinion is as gooa pollaticks.

Th' English cup's left Lankisher ! There owt to be three months 0' general mournin', etsettera, to celebrate th' event. Id owt to be cele- brated wi' gret rejoicin', becose there'll happen be a end o' th' excitement, an bettin' an' boozin' as he olez bin connected wi' footbo'. Eh,dear, times isn'd as they used to be, an' some fooak doesn'd seem to think as they ever con be th' same ageean,sooa they ne'er try to mek 'em th'sarne; they think becose we hey steeam engines, an' tallygraffs, as we mon keep whizz& on at th' speed we are, an' bother abeawt , nowt nobbut mekkin' brass an' spendin' id—kiln' thersels to keep thersels. Well, it's a gret mis- take, an' mooast o' fooak doesn'd find id eawt till it's towd 'em bi th' doctor, an' it's too late to stert o'er agean then ; an' their childer learn nowt bi id. Just think heaw mich different things wod be i' Lankisher—an' through England—iv we went back to eawr gret-gronfayther's days au' cus- toms bi keepin' up May day i' th' good owd style; there's lots o' bonny lasses to pick a May Queen fro', an' as for rush carts, Robin Hood, Friar Tuck, morris dancers, quarter-staff players,an' everything else as is wanted, aw think they con be raised wi' a bit a tryin'. Th' top an' bottom on't is, we're o' on us geddin' too serious,an' we find as we're owd men afoore we're gradely young ; it's cram, cram, cram, an' wear an' tear to pass full time, an' then it's werk,werk,werk, woss nor slaves, fro' leeavin' skoo' to th' funeral service bein' read o'er us, an' herdly a atom o' real pleasure in between. "Merry England !" Wod onybody i' their reight senses co' England merry neawdays ? It's just abeawt as merry as a chap is when he hes th' tooth- werch gradely bad, or as a chap as hes just dropt his life's savin's in a rotten buildin' society. Merry,eh ! Stop an' think for tooathri minutes wod th' princi- pal spoorts is wi' mooast fooak. Billiards for chaps, an' dancin' for booath wimmen an men, i' hot, clooase rooms, th' wimmen nobbut hofe drest. Nice recreation, is'nd id ? Oh, ay, aw know as aw've mentioned footbo', an' as they play at bat an' bo', but heaw do they play at booath ? Do they play for th' pleasure o'th game., or for th' good i d'll do em? Nod they ! A lot on ern plays to win, an' nowt else, an' they'll do o' soorts o' lungeus werk an' shabby tricks forth' sake o' wi unite ; an' another lot on em play becose they ged paid for playin',— it's their werk, an' nod play, for they hey to mek their livin' by id. Tek race runners,too ; they keer nowt abeawt nowt else but runnin' a querter mile i'th' twentieth pert ov a seckond less no somebody else hes run id in, an' they'll brast a blood vessel an , kill thersels to do this. Ov course there's a tooathri ,as doesn'd gooa in for this style o' racin' but pre- fers thad soort wheer they hey to creep through drain pipes, scrat th' skin off their faces wi' jumpin through thorn hedges, an' spoil their clooas i climbin' o'er top o' tar barrels. Aw see nowt wiling doin' these things, wen a bull's alter yo, but to pay a entrance fee for th' sake o' bein' alleawed to do id is th' silliest trick as aw ever heeard on. Neaw then, yo chaps on Sports Committees, con yo nod chuck eawt o these senseless events, an' put sum- mat in their place at's innicent, monly, an' merry? Just put yo'r heyds together, an' see iv a beawt at querter-staff wodn'd be better, an' mek just as mich gam for th' spectators. But yo may telt my word for id we shall mek no gret discovery th' *ay we're goin' on; railway trains an' steamers may run into one another through th' madmen as hes to do wi' em, but there'll be no soort of discovery med through thad,nobbut as th' deeath rate is bigger nor id wor. Gooa back to th' owd style o' spoorts, an' iv yo dorn'd find yo'rsels merrier, strunger, an' bet- ter altogether for id ray name is'nd wod id is.
THE DURHAM STRIKE.
At a meeting of Durham miners, on Saturday, resolu- tions were passed empowering the Federation Board to again meet the colliery owners with a view to effecting a settlement.

The result of the Durham colliers' ballot on the ques- tion of continuing the strike or allowing the Federation Board to approach the colliery owners with a view to a settlement of the dispute has not yet been officially de- clared, but the information obtainei shows an over- whelming majority against the proposals of the Board. The figures published on Wednesday gave a majority of nearly five to one in favour of carrying on the strike.

div.head: SHIPPING SHIPPING TRADE.
div.p: THE SHIPPING SHIPPING TRADE.

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach received at the Board of Trade on Wednesday, a deputation introduced by Mr. Chamberlain, including sailor, representatives of every port in the kingdom, in favour of a Bill introduced by Mr. Howell to amend the Merchant Shipping Act by pre- venting vessels going to sea when the load-line is sub- merged,and also providing for the inspection of seamen's food. Sir Michael expressed approval of the principle of the clause as to the load-line, and said he thought an inspection of sailors' food might be extended to ocean- going ships. Subject to some amendments of procedure, he favoured the Bill generally, and hoped it would pass with the assent of respectable shipowners, who admit- tedly needed no such legislation.

A POLICE COURT MISSIONARY FOR W,A.R 12,1 N uTo N, WIDNES, &c. As will be seen by an advertisement, a meeting will be held in the Masonic Rooms, Warrington, on Tuesday next, at three o'clock over which the Rector of Warrington will preside. The object is to interest the people of the town and neighbourhood in the scheme to appoint a missionary to visit the War- rington, Widnes, and Newton Police Courts under the direction of the Diocesan C.E.T.S. The pro- posal is in connection with the Clarke Aspinall Tem- perance Memorial, its object being to appoint five more Police Court Missionaries to labour in Liver- pool and the large towns of the diocese in com- memoration of the work of the late Mr. Clarke Aspinall J.P., Coroner of Liverpool and Chairman of the Diocesan Church of England Temperance Society. The speakers will be the Rev. Canon Blundell, Rector of Ilalsall, Ormskirk, and lion. Chaplain to the Queen, the Rev. .1. Hirst, Diocesan Secretary, and William C. Procter, Esq., a Liver- , pool merchant, and treasurer of the fund, all of whom are well acquainted with the work. It will possibly be asked what the duties are of such a missionary. It would therefore be well to explain how a similar work has been carried on for 12 years past i)y the same Society in Liverpool. The mission- ary attends the Court, and watches the cases as they come on speaks to the men and women, who have been fined for drunkenness, &c, as they leave the Court, descends into the cells to converse with prisoners when asked by a magistrate ; visits inebriates in their homes, Sze. Mr. Justice Denman says:—" If you catch a young man or young girl at the door of a police court, after re- ceiving a mere nominal punishment or no punish-' merit at all, for a first offence, and can instil into the mind of that young person what will come to him or her—what is likely to be the result of it if they allow themselves to be there again by not be- ing able to say No ' to such a question as, 'Come and have a drink '—it is incalculable how much good may be done—not only to them but to the whole community." This was a work which the late Mr. Aspinull much appreciated. As a lay magis- trate of the city of Liverpool, he voluntarily under- took to try the cases in what was known as the "Drunkards' "court every morning. In this way the useful work of the missionaries of the Society was observed by hi m,and much appreciated. To meet the cost of such an agent a sum of £l5O per year will be needed for salary, travelling expenses, &c. It is to be hoped that the Memorial Committee will not appeal in vain. It is a work which ought to receive the support of both Conformists and Non- conformists as those oj any or no religion are helped.

div.head: GREAT STOPPAGE OF COTTON MILLS.
div.p: GREAT STOPPAGE OF COTTON MILLS.

The Cotton Masters' Federation, at a meeting at Man- chester, yesterday afternoon, unanimously decided to close their mills at Ashton, Stalybridge, Oldham, Moss- ley. Hyde. Heywood, Rochdale, and Stockport, the stoppage commencing on the 16th inst., and will con- tinue until the termination of the Stalybridge strike, which has lasted sixteen weeks. DEEMING'S PENDING TRIAL. THE LANDING AT MELBOURNE.

MELBOURNE, FRMAL—TIie P. and 0. steamer Ballarat, with Deeming, alias Williams, on board, arrived in the bay here at eleven o'clock this morning. Be was con- veyed direct to the City Police Court, adjoining the gaol, where he was charged with the murder of his wife, known as Mrs. Williams, at Windsor, on December 24th last. After the police had given formal evidence as to the issue of the warrant and the arrest, the prisoner was remanded. for a week. He was then removed to the gaol, outside which immense crowds had assembled in anticipation of Deeming's arrival. The people hooted and hissed loudly, but were otherwise orderly. The prisoner who, during the voyage of the Ballarat,showed for the most part a cheerful disposition, began to display considerable apprehension as the vessel neared Mel- bourne, and repeatedly asked the officers in charge of him to take precautions to avoid the crowd.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at 4.15. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord SALISBURY in reply to Lord Kimberley said the House would adjourn on Thursday until the 2nd of May. Lord Denman's motion to read a second time the Duration of Speeches in House of Lord's Bill was negatived. The Local Authorities Acquisition of Land Bill was read a second time, and the Hares Bill was read a third time. _

The House adjourned at 4.50. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at 2.5 p.m. The Leeds and Liverpool Canal Bill was read a third time. BIRTHS ix Paisox.—Mr. MATTHEWS in answer to Mr. Campbell said that during the last financial year for which statistics are available the number of women released from prison before the expiration of their sen- tences on account of advanced pregnancy was not 68 but 12. In these cases the probable date of their con- iinement was such that if allowed to take place in prison they would have had to remain there after the expira- tion of their sentence. THE INFLUX OF FOREIGN PATIPERS.—Mr. J. LOWTHER asked whether in view of information to the effect that the exodus Of destitute persons from Russia is expected in well-informed quarters to assume extended proportions in the near future, it was the intention of Her Majesty's Government to introduce a bill to prohibit the admis- sion into the United Kingdom of all persons likely to become a public charge, or to increase the difficulties of obtaining a livelihood already pressing upon large num- bers of the native labouring population in this country. Mr. BALFOUR said nothing had occurred that would justify the introduction of a Bill such as was suggested by his right hon. friend. The Government quite appre- ciated the gravity of the matter and were watching it most carefully. They felt that such an invasion as was suggested would be an intolerable abuse of the system of emigration. _ _ _

GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS TO FORM:MRS.—Mr. JAMES LOWTHER asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether, inasmuch as the practice of giving contracts to foreign manufacturers for the supply of pencils, matches, and other articles used by the public departments involved a contravention of the resolution passed by the House of Commons on February 13, 1891, the Government would, in view of the serious depression prevailing in so many home industries make it a condition that all such contracts ;hall be executed within the British Empire. Mr. BALFOUR said that undoubtedly it was a good principle to rely upon native industry as far as possible, but it would hardly be just to the taxpayers of the country to make a practice of buying in the most expensive market in order to do this. —Mr.'Lowrwita said he would again call attention to the matter.

BELLIGERENT ORANGE/MEN.—Mr. SEXTON asked a ques- tion as to the recent alleged inflammatory utterances at a political meeting of Lord Arthur Hill, Comptroller of the Household, and failing to obtain what he considered a satisfactory answer gays notice that he should move that the resolutions passed at the meeting in question, which consisted of Irish Conservatives, be laid on the table of the House.

Tag PALACE RATCATCHER.—The House having gone into Committee of Supply on the vote of £29,850 for Royal Palaces and Marlborough House, Mr. Morton pro- tested against the excessive cost of the repairs of these establishments, and called attention to two items to which he also took exception, namely, £270 for coal, light, water, and household expenses, and £1 Bs. per week for a turncock, who also received LB a year for acting as ratcatcher at Buckingham Palace —Mr. PLoNEET said the first item represented coal,light, as the officials appointed by the Board of Works' and the ratcatcher's allowance of course was to prevent vermin destroying the building—Mr. LABOUCHERE had no objection to the ratcatcher. He thought he might be brought down to the House of Commons, and on that side of the House he might be able to catch some- thing.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS. Lamm Ar7l3 GELTLEMEN, —Your votes and interests are :respectfully solicited on behalf of the 'following Four Candi- dates. brought forward by the Ratepayers' Associatson ; viz. : Messrs. CARROLL, GERRA.RD. SMITH, and SINGLETON, . all of whom are residents in the town, and well known to • most of you. Several candidates appeal to you on the ground that they are " old members" of the Board—so old in fact, as to have forgotten who sent them there, as 'witness the treatment of many tradesmen re the unjust minimum water charge, and the ' scant courtesy accorded to the mem- bers of the Widnes Trades Council, when applying to have the non-sweating clause inserted in the Board's contracts. You have now the opportunity of putting men .on the Board who are get-at-able, and who, if elected, will do their beat to serve you and the town in which they live. Vote as you voted at the last election, and the above four Candidates will head the poll. Signed on behalf of the Widnes Ratepayers' Association. 4V. CHRISTIE, Hon. Sec. Committee Rooms, 83, Victoria-road.

WIDNES LOC L BOARD ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELEuTORS. GENTLEMEN,-A large number of Workingmen have requested me to allow myself to be nominated as a Candidate for the forthcoming Election. This I promised to do, but only in case the retiring mem- bers were opposed by any other persons, as 1 felt it would be better to avoid the expenses of an election until we obtain our Charter of Incorporation. However, a contest has been forced upon us by the " Rate- payers' " and" Owners' and Occupiers' "Associations, and as neither of these bodies have shown themselves very favourable to the interests of the Working Classes, it is but just that they should have a representative to express their views and to enforce them as far as possible. This I will endeavour to do if returned as a Member of the Looal.Board. In sympathy with the majority of our townspeople, I most decidedly object to the Board giving any contracts out of the district, and especially where the work can be done equally as well by resident tradesmen. It is neither charitable, honest, nor just, to employ workers from outside, while we have hundreds of men idle in the town who have to pauperise themselves and families to exist. I solicit your votes as a protest against the contemptuous manner your appeal through the Trades' Council was treated by the Members of th 3 Local Board.—Yeurs truly, JOHN"WILLIAMSON.

• COUNTY OF CHESTER. _NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be held at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in the said County on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-men- tioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Cltrk of the Peace. Chester, 14th March, 1892.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 AND 1886. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. THE CHESHIRE MARKETS AND FAIRS (FOOT-AND- MOUTH DISEASE) ORDER OF 1892. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of this County, at a Meeting held on Saturday, the 26th day of March instant, decided, pursuant to Article 5 of the above Order, to GRANT LICENSES FOR THE HOLDING OF PUBLIC SALES, on and after the 4th day of April next, of Fat Cattle, or Fat Sheep, or Fat Swine for immediate Slaughter, on the following conditions, viz. : (a) That the Cattle, Sheep, and Swine, exposed at the public sale so licensed, shall, after their arrival thereat, and before they are moved therefrom, be marked by and at the expense of the owner, con- signee, or other person exposing them as follows : CATTLE.—By the clipping of a broad arrow, about five inches long, on the left hind quarter of each of the Cattle. . SHEEP AND SWINE.—By the painting or stamping of the letter M about six inches long, on the left side of each of the Sheep and Swine with the following composition, namely :—Rosin, five parts; oil of turpentine, two parts; and blue or red orchre, one part ; melted and used warm ; or with some other adhesive composition of a blue or red colour. (b) Every head of Cattle, and every Sheep, and every Pig, that is exposed at the public sale so licensed whether it is sold thereat or not, shall be moved from the premises where such public sale has been held along the nearest public road direct to some Slaughter-house, from which Slaughter-house they shall not be again removed,but shall be slaughtered there within a period of 72 hours, and shall be kept isolated from any other Animals not intended to be slaughtered within such period. (c) Cattle, Sheep, and Swine, exposed at the public sale so licensed, shall not afterwards be exposed at any other public sale. Forms of applications for Licenses may be obtained from the Local inspector of the District in which the ' Proposed sale is intended to be held, and must be de- livered to him not later than p.m. on the Wednesday in the week previous to that in which the sale is pro- posed to be held. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 28th March, 1892.
